complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The map $\theta\mapsto J(\theta,\phi(\theta))$ is $C^1$. By [F2], its derivative at $\theta_0$ is $J_\theta+J_zD\phi$. Substituting step 1.1 yields $J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: The map $\theta\mapsto J(\theta,\phi(\theta))$ is $C^1$. By [F2], its derivative at $\theta_0$ is $J_\theta+J_zD\phi$. Substituting step 1.1 yields $J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Since $R_z$ is invertible, $R_z^T$ is invertible. The adjoint equation has the unique solution satisfying $\lambda^T=J_zR_z^{-1}$, by transposing $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$. Therefore $J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta=\lambda^TR_\theta$, giving the stated adjoint formula. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Since $R_z$ is invertible, $R_z^T$ is invertible. The adjoint equation has the unique solution satisfying $\lambda^T=J_zR_z^{-1}$, by transposing $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$. Therefore $J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta=\lambda^TR_\theta$, giving the stated adjoint formula.

items.assessment: The Definition supplies a finite admissible graph and direction, initializes input tangents, and applies each exact primitive derivative to its parent tuple. If the output is an input it returns that coordinate direction directly, including no-operation graphs. Domain failures and nonunique strict branches return statuses, not an arbitrary derivative choice.

claim_sections.Definition:
Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]], an admissible point $x$, and a direction $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Evaluate all primal node values in topological order and store the tape. Set each input tangent to $\dot x_i=v_i$. For each operation $j=1,\ldots,T$, compute
$$\dot z_j=D\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})(\dot z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,\dot z_{p_{j,r_j}}).$$
Return the primal scalar output $f(x)$ and its tangent: return $(z_o,\dot z_o)$ if $o$ is an operation node, and $(x_i,v_i)$ if $o$ is input coordinate $i$. If the input is outside the admissible domain, return DOMAIN_ERROR; if a piecewise primitive is at a branch boundary or has no unique strict active branch, return NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no tangent. All derivative evaluations in this definition are exact real-arithmetic operations on the specified primitive maps.

items.assessment: The Definition zero-initializes all accumulators, seeds only the designated scalar output and processes every parent slot in fixed reverse order. Repeated slots contribute separately; an input output returns the identity coordinate seed even with no operations. It differentiates a strict real graph only and returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE at a switch, not an iff or chosen subgradient.

claim_sections.Definition:
Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]] and an admissible point $x$. Evaluate and store all primal values in topological order. Initialize every operation cotangent and every input cotangent to zero. Seed the scalar output by setting its cotangent to $1$: if $o$ is an operation, set $\bar z_o=1$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $\bar x_i=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, compute the contribution
$$c_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})^T\bar z_j$$
and add it to the cotangent accumulator of that parent: use $\bar x_i$ if the parent is input coordinate $i$, and $\bar z_\ell$ if it is operation node $\ell$. If the same parent node occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution. Return the scalar output $f(x)$ and the input cotangents $(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n)$ as the Euclidean gradient. A point outside the admissible domain returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. The procedure differentiates the real-arithmetic graph; it makes no floating-point error claim.

items.assessment: The proof begins with the whole input space and builds admissible domains by finite preimages of primitive open domains, then applies the chain rule. An input-coordinate output is covered with no operation node; an empty admissible open set makes the local assertion vacuous. Strict branch boundaries are excluded from the derivative conclusion, with no arbitrary primitive/branch selection.

claim_sections.Statement: For a finite straight-line program whose primitives are $C^1$, the recursively defined admissible input domain is open on each fixed strict branch. The scalar output $f$ is $C^1$ there, and its total derivative is obtained by the ordinary chain rule through the primitive maps.

Thus $\Omega_j:=\{x\in\Omega_{j-1}:g_j(x)\in U_j\}$ is open in $\Omega_{j-1}$, hence open in $\mathbb R^n$, because $U_j$ is open. This proves by finite induction that the full admissible domain is open. [F1, F3, given, construct]

claim_sections.Statement: If every primitive of a finite straight-line program is $C^2$ on the selected open branch domains, then the real-arithmetic scalar output is $C^2$ on each fixed strict branch.

The scalar output is therefore $C^2$ whether it is one of these values or an input coordinate projection. On a strict branch the selected primitive maps stay fixed on an open neighborhood; no claim is made at branch switches.

items.assessment: The Definition returns starting state and unchanged supplied cotangent on an empty transition interval. Positive uniform mode requires positive snapshot budget; binomial mode explicitly handles lengths zero and one before recursive splitting, so zero resource budgets are only admitted at capacity-one leaves. Replay maps/order/domains are fixed and no schedule optimality or arbitrary branch choice is asserted.

claim_sections.Definition:
The input is a finite sequence of deterministic $C^1$ transitions $F_1,\ldots,F_T$ between open subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, with starting state $x_0$. Every transition is evaluated on one fixed strict branch and has its exact local reverse rule. The last transition has scalar output and may be the terminal objective, so its scalar cotangent is $1$; for an empty sequence the terminal value is the starting state. A transition tape stores the local values needed by its exact reverse rule. A deterministic replay applies the same transition maps, in the same order, to the identical checkpoint state and therefore reproduces the same values and local derivative inputs. The procedure returns the terminal output and cotangent at $x_0$; an invalid domain evaluation returns DOMAIN_ERROR, and a branch boundary returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE. A checkpoint schedule is permitted only when its saved states and all deterministic replays lie in these declared domains.

**Uniform-block mode.** For $T=0$, return $x_0$ and the supplied cotangent without work. For $T\ge1$, require an integer slot budget $m\ge1$, set $q=\lceil T/m\rceil$, and during one forward pass save $x_{jq}$ for $j=0,\ldots,\lceil T/q\rceil-1$ (all indices are below $T$). This uses at most $m$ saved states. Partition the steps into blocks $[a,b]$ with $a=jq$ and $b=\min(a+q,T)$. Process the blocks from last to first. Within one block, for $\ell=b,b-1,\ldots,a+1$, restore $x_a$, replay $F_{a+1},\ldots,F_{\ell-1}$ without recording, evaluate $F_\ell$ once while recording its local tape, apply its reverse rule to the current cotangent, and discard the one-step tape and replay workspace. Retain only the checkpoint states, the live state/cotangent, and the ordinary one-step reverse tape. Do not infer any optimality property of this schedule.

**Binomial mode.** Define $C(d,0)=C(0,t)=1$, and $C(d,t)=C(d-1,t)+C(d,t-1)$ for integers $d,t\ge1$. The recursive procedure REVERSE$(a,N,d,t,x_a,\bar x_{a+N})$ requires integer indices $0\le a\le a+N\le T$, nonnegative integer budgets $d,t$, the capacity condition $N\le C(d,t)$, and a known starting state $x_a$. If $N=0$, return the pair $(x_a,\bar x_a)$, the known terminal state and unchanged cotangent. If $N=1$, evaluate and record the unique transition, apply its local reverse rule, and return its output and input cotangents. If $N\ge2$, then $d,t\ge1$. Put $L=\min(N-1,C(d,t-1))$, $R=N-L$; replay the first $L$ transitions from $x_a$ without recording and save the resulting midpoint state $x_{a+L}$. Call REVERSE$(a+L,R,d-1,t,x_{a+L},\bar x_{a+N})$ on the right block. Release the midpoint checkpoint, restore the caller's supplied $x_a$, and call REVERSE$(a,L,d,t-1,x_a,\bar x_{a+L})$ on the left block, where $\bar x_{a+L}$ is the cotangent returned by the right call. Return the right call's terminal value and the left call's cotangent at $x_a$. The top-level call uses $a=0,N=T$, with the specified terminal cotangent. A recursive call with $N>1$ and $d=0$ or $t=0$ is a schedule failure; the capacity condition makes that branch unreachable.

The parameter $d$ bounds the number of simultaneously saved state snapshots. The parameter $t$ bounds, for each transition, the number of additional unrecorded forward evaluations beyond its one recorded evaluation. Both are finite integer inputs. This mode gives a binomial capacity bound; it does not promise a numerical error estimate or an optimal schedule for arbitrary nonuniform primitive costs. For the storage count in the paired theorem, $R_s$ bounds scalar storage for one full primal state. The binomial recursion may reuse one mutable cotangent workspace: each call consumes its terminal cotangent and returns the cotangent at its start, reusing the same buffer through both children. Let $G$ bound the largest one-step tape and local reverse scratch, the constant number of live cotangent/work vectors, and the scalar call-frame records; it excludes the $d$ saved primal states and one live primal state.

items.assessment: The Definition admits zero iteration, state and parameter dimensions. Budget zero evaluates only the initial map; empty coordinate loops return the required empty Jacobian shape while still evaluating primal recursion. It computes the specified finite map and propagates domain/branch failures, not a selected exact fixed point or an iff about residual convergence.

claim_sections.Definition:
Input a finite-dimensional $C^1$ map $G(z,\theta)$, a $C^1$ initial-state map $z_0(\theta)$, a parameter $\theta$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^p$, and an integer budget $K\ge0$; the states lie in $\mathbb R^m$, with $p,m\ge0$. Use the specified maps $z_0$ and $G$, with their exact derivative evaluations, as primitive maps on their declared open domains. Evaluate $z_0(\theta)$ and then $z_{k+1}(\theta)=G(z_k(\theta),\theta)$ for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$. A primitive-domain failure returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no derivative. The admissible case requires every evaluation to remain in its declared domain and, for piecewise primitives, on a unique strict active branch.

Allocate an $m\times p$ Jacobian array $J$. For each state coordinate $a=1,\ldots,m$, form the finite scalar-output graph for $f_a(\theta)=(z_K(\theta))_a$ by appending the coordinate projection to the finite recursion. For each parameter coordinate $\ell=1,\ldots,p$, call [[alg-forward-mode-automatic-differentiation]] on this graph at $\theta$ with direction $e_\ell$, the $\ell$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^p$, and put its returned tangent in $J_{a\ell}$. Propagate any DOMAIN_ERROR or NONDIFFERENTIABLE status from a call. Return $(z_K(\theta),J)$ with status ITERATES_DIFFERENTIATED. For $K=0$ the recursion contains only the initial-state map. If $m=0$ or $p=0$, the corresponding loops are empty and $J$ has the specified empty shape; the primal recursion is still evaluated. This procedure differentiates the $K$-step map actually specified by $G,z_0,K$; it does not substitute the derivative of an exact fixed point.

items.assessment: The Definition seeds cotangent/tangent-cotangent (1,0), differentiates each exact reverse contribution and accumulates repeated parent slots separately. An input-coordinate output has constant gradient and zero tangent-cotangent; no-operation or zero directions require no special derivative choice. Its strict C2 graph/domain requirements exclude branch switches.

claim_sections.Definition:
Input a $C^2$ graph, admissible $x$, and direction $v$. First run the forward tangent recurrence to compute every $\dot z_j=Dz_j(x)v$. Initialize every operation and input cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulator to zero. Seed the output by setting its cotangent/tangent-cotangent pair to $(1,0)$: if $o$ is an operation, set $(\bar z_o,\dot{\bar z}_o)=(1,0)$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)=(1,0)$. In reverse topological order, for each node $j$ and parent slot $k$, let $A_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$, compute
$$c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\bar z_j,\qquad \dot c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\dot{\bar z}_j+\bigl(DA_{j,k}(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})[\dot z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,\dot z_{p_{j,r_j}}]\bigr)^{T}\bar z_j,$$
and add $c_{j,k}$ and $\dot c_{j,k}$ to the parent's cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulators. Use $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)$ for input coordinate $i$ and $(\bar z_\ell,\dot{\bar z}_\ell)$ for operation node $\ell$. If the same parent occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution.
Return the input tangent of the gradient, $(\dot{\bar x}_1,\ldots,\dot{\bar x}_n)$. Repeated parent slots receive separate additions. Outside the admissible domain return DOMAIN_ERROR; at a branch boundary return NONDIFFERENTIABLE. The transpose is the real Euclidean transpose, not a complex adjoint.

items.assessment: The proof checks input-coordinate tangents first, inducts exact primitive compositions, and explicitly handles either operation output or input output. Empty operation lists and zero direction retain the corresponding coordinate derivative/zero tangent. This is correctness on a supplied strict graph, not an iff or arbitrary choice of a branch.

claim_sections.Statement: Let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the output of a finite $C^1$ program on a fixed strict branch. For every admissible $x\in\Omega$ and direction $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the forward-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)v$.

items.assessment: The proof expands prescribed parent-slot paths, with a length-zero identity path at the output and zero sum when no path exists. Thus empty outgoing families, disconnected nodes and input-coordinate outputs are covered by the seed/zero initialization. Exact graph correctness is a direct implication, with no interval endpoint or arbitrary path selection principle.

claim_sections.Statement: For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix a node $i$ and form the downstream map $F_i(u)$ by replacing its value with an independent $u$ while holding earlier node values fixed and then evaluating later operations in topological order. At each operation, its derivative is linear in the concatenated parent direction, so contributions from distinct parent slots add. If $i=o$, the output is $u$ and the length-zero path contributes the identity; if there is no path from $i$ to $o$, $F_i$ is locally constant and the sum is zero. items.assessment: The Statement counts arithmetic work for a supplied finite primitive graph and includes buffer initialization in storage, not arithmetic. With no operation nodes the work sum is zero; input-gradient storage remains in S. The proof separately sums fixed primal/pullback/parent costs and excludes opaque calls lacking those ratios, rather than claiming an iff or arbitrary solver choice.

claim_sections.Statement: Fix a finite set of scalar/vector primitive types with at most $r$ parent slots per operation. Suppose each operation $j$ has primal work $w_j\ge1$, its local vector-Jacobian product costs at most $c w_j$, and accumulating each parent-slot contribution costs at most $a$ operations. Count all state-vector dimensions and input-gradient entries in the primal-tape size $S$. Then the exact reverse-mode algorithm for a scalar output uses at most $(1+c+ar)\sum_{j=1}^T w_j$ operations for the primal evaluation, reverse sweep, and parent accumulations, and stores $O(S)$ scalar entries. Opaque solver calls are excluded unless their primal and derivative costs satisfy the same hypotheses.
claim_sections.Remarks: Baur–Strassen proves a separate nonscalar arithmetic-circuit complexity theorem over an infinite field. The local bound above is proved directly for a fixed smooth primitive set with explicit primal/pullback cost ratios; it does not extend the arithmetic-circuit theorem to arbitrary opaque procedures or claim that every differentiable primitive has a cheap derivative.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The primal pass evaluates each node once, so its cost is $\sum_j w_j=W$. The reverse pass makes one local pullback call at node $j$, costing at most $c w_j$, and handles at most $r$ parent slots, costing at most $ar$ arithmetic operations. Since $w_j\ge1$, this node's reverse arithmetic work is at most $(c+ar)w_j$. Summing over all nodes gives total arithmetic work at most $(1+c+ar)W$; cotangent-buffer initialization is storage under [A2]. [F1, F2, A1, A2, given, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The primal tape contains the recorded graph values and fixed-size node/parent metadata; by the definition of $S$, this is $O(S)$ scalar entries. Reverse cotangents require one vector of the corresponding dimension per node and one input-gradient vector, all dimensions already counted in $S$. Bounded primitive workspace adds at most $O(S)$ entries. Hence total storage is $O(S)$; the bound says nothing about an opaque solver whose local tape or pullback cost was excluded in [A1]. items.assessment: The proof explicitly treats empty reversed intervals as unchanged state/cotangent and one-step intervals as one exact local tape. Positive uniform mode uses finite block lengths; binomial recursion has stated capacity and decreasing child resources. The schedule and replays are deterministic, and the theorem proves correctness/cost bounds without claiming optimality or a selected schedule family.

claim_sections.Statement: For the finite-dimensional $C^1$ transition sequences on a fixed strict branch defined in [[alg-checkpointed-reverse-schedules]], provided every schedule replay remains in the declared domains, both schedules return the same terminal value and initial-state cotangent as an uncheckpointed reverse sweep. In uniform-block mode, if $T,m\ge1$, $q=\lceil T/m\rceil$, and the block lengths are $r_1,\ldots,r_s$, the number of additional unrecorded forward evaluations is exactly $\sum_{\ell=1}^s r_\ell(r_\ell-1)/2$, at most $m q(q-1)/2$. At most $m$ checkpoint states are saved, with one live replay state and one local step tape. In binomial mode, $C(d,t)=\binom{d+t}{d}$; any $T\le C(d,t)$ steps can be reversed with at most $d$ saved snapshots, one recorded forward evaluation and one reverse evaluation per step, at most $t$ additional unrecorded forward evaluations per step, total work at most $\widehat W+\overline W+tW$, and storage $G+(d+1)R_s$. Here $W$ is the total cost of one unrecorded full forward pass, $\widehat W$ the sum of recorded one-step forward costs, $\overline W$ the sum of local reverse costs, $R_s$ bounds scalar storage for one primal state, and $G$ bounds the largest one-step tape and local reverse scratch, the constant number of live cotangent/work vectors, and scalar recursion-frame records, excluding saved states and one live primal state.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: In uniform mode, for any block start $x_a$, deterministic replay reproduces the original $x_{a+1},\ldots,x_b$: the first replayed transition starts from the identical $x_a$, and induction applies each same map $F_j$ to the same preceding state. Thus the recorded local tape at step $\ell$ has the same primitive inputs as the original forward trajectory, so its reverse rule is the same one used by the full tape. Processing blocks and then their steps in decreasing order is exactly reverse transition order; [F2] gives the same terminal and initial cotangents. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

The proof differentiates the finite recurrence and sums its error propagation, then gives a concrete zero-residual example with nonzero finite-derivative discrepancy. It is not an iff or an unqualified residual-only derivative certificate; all neighborhoods/maps are supplied.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $G(z,\theta)$ be $C^2$ near $(z_*,\theta_0)$, with $z_*=G(z_*,\theta_0)$. Let $D$ be an open convex state neighborhood of $z_*$ on which $G$ is defined and $C^2$ near $D\times\{\theta_0\}$. Assume $G(D,\theta_0)\subseteq D$, $\|G_z(z,\theta_0)\|\le q<1$, and $G_z,G_\theta$ are Lipschitz in $z$ with constants $L_z,L_\theta$. Let the initial map $z_0(\theta)$ be $C^1$ and its iterates remain in $D$. Write $s_*=D\phi(\theta_0)$ for the local exact fixed-point branch supplied by the implicit function theorem, $e_k=D_\theta z_k(\theta_0)$, $\delta_0=\|z_0(\theta_0)-z_*\|$, $d_0=\|e_0-s_*\|$, and $C=L_z\|s_*\|+L_\theta$. For every integer $K\ge1$,
$$\|z_K(\theta_0)-z_*\|\le q^K\delta_0,\qquad \|e_K-s_*\|\le q^K d_0+C K q^{K-1}\delta_0,$$

items.assessment: The proof differentiates the exact reverse recurrence of a strict finite C2 graph using the product rule. An input-coordinate output is explicitly treated as constant gradient with zero Hessian-vector output; a zero direction also propagates zero through the linearized recurrence. No Hessian-symmetry, branch-switch derivative or arbitrary map selection is assumed.

claim_sections.Statement: Let $f$ be the scalar output of a finite $C^2$ graph on a fixed strict branch. At every admissible $x$ and direction $v$, the forward-over-reverse algorithm returns $D(\operatorname{grad} f)(x)v$, the Hessian-vector product $H_f(x)v$. No Hessian symmetry assumption is needed for this identity.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [F4], the input reverse accumulator is the function $x\mapsto\operatorname{grad} f(x)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$ by [F2] under the primitive hypotheses in [F1], its directional derivative at $x$ exists. By [F3], the forward recurrence supplies every primitive-input direction $\dot z_{pa}=Dz_{pa}(x)v$. [F2, F3, F4, given]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [F4], the input reverse accumulator is the function $x\mapsto\operatorname{grad} f(x)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$ by [F2] under the primitive hypotheses in [F1], its directional derivative at $x$ exists. By [F3], the forward recurrence supplies every primitive-input direction $\dot z_{pa}=Dz_{pa}(x)v$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At a node $j$, the exact reverse contribution to parent slot $i$ is $A^T\bar z_j$. Since each primitive is $C^2$, $A$ is $C^1$; the finite reverse recurrence is therefore differentiable, as it consists of sums and bounded bilinear matrix-vector products of $C^1$ maps. Differentiate this matrix-vector product along $x+tv$. The product rule [F6] gives $A^T\dot{\bar z}_j+(DA[\dot z_{pa}])^T\bar z_j$, exactly the second recurrence in [F5]. Reverse topological induction therefore shows that every $\dot{\bar z}_i$ equals the directional derivative of the corresponding exact reverse accumulator. If the scalar output is an input coordinate, its seeded gradient is the constant coordinate vector and the initialized tangent-cotangent remains zero, as this recurrence also gives. [F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

items.assessment: The proof expands the given finite strict graph into paths, interpreting the length-zero output path as identity and disconnected-input path sums as zero. Empty prefix/suffix matrix products are identities in telescoping each path. The output seed is unchanged, so those empty terms add no error; exact reverse accumulation is required and no arbitrary error family is selected.

claim_sections.Statement:
For a finite scalar-output graph on one fixed strict branch, associate to each parent-slot edge $e$ the exact local derivative map $A_e$ at the exact real-arithmetic primal values. Suppose a reverse recurrence instead uses local maps $\widetilde A_e$ from the same branch satisfying $\|\widetilde A_e-A_e\|\le\eta_e$, with exact accumulation arithmetic. For an input block $i$, let $\mathcal P(i,o)$ be the finite directed paths from that block to output $o$, and order the edges of a path $\pi=(e_1,\ldots,e_s)$ from input to output. The exact gradient contribution is the transpose of $A_{e_s}\cdots A_{e_1}$, and the perturbed recurrence returns the corresponding sum using $\widetilde A_e$. It obeys
$$\|\widetilde g_i-g_i\|\le\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P(i,o)}\sum_{\ell=1}^s\eta_{e_\ell}\left(\prod_{r<\ell}\|A_{e_r}\|\right)\left(\prod_{r>\ell}(\|A_{e_r}\|+\eta_{e_r})\right).$$
The bound covers local Jacobian and derivative-evaluation errors represented by $\eta_e$. It does not include roundoff in the reverse accumulation additions.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Starting with output cotangent $1$, the exact reverse recurrence at a node sums one local derivative-transpose contribution from each outgoing parent-slot edge. By induction in reverse topological order, its expansion at input block $i$ has one ordered derivative product for every path from $i$ to the output: the length-zero path at the output node has product $1$ (including when the output itself is an input), and extending a path by one edge multiplies its product by that edge's local derivative. The same finite recurrence with $\widetilde A_e$ yields the sum of perturbed path products; the output seed is unchanged. By [F2], the exact path sum is $g_i$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

The same finite recurrence with $\widetilde A_e$ yields the sum of perturbed path products; the output seed is unchanged. By [F2], the exact path sum is $g_i$.

items.assessment: The scalar example gives exactly two strict formulas with derivatives plus/minus one. At zero the one-sided quotients differ, so the prescribed status is NONDIFFERENTIABLE rather than a chosen subgradient. There is one fixed nonempty primitive input, no continuous interval endpoint outside the switch analysis and no biconditional theorem.

claim_sections.Example: The primitive $f(x)=|x|$ has two strict branches: $f(x)=x$ for $x>0$ and $f(x)=-x$ for $x<0$. Branchwise AD returns derivative $1$ on the positive branch and $-1$ on the negative branch. At the switch $x=0$ it returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At zero, the right difference quotient is $(|h|-0)/h=1$ for $h>0$, while the left quotient is $(|h|-0)/h=-1$ for $h<0$. Since the one-sided limits differ, the derivative does not exist at zero. [given, algebra]

items.assessment: The example fixes two scalar Euler steps, a positive half-step and initial state one. Verification computes both forward tape and reverse contributions at parameter one, giving three halves, with fixed unit output seed. It does not vary the number of steps to empty or choose a trajectory/adjoint from a family.

claim_sections.Example:
Take two explicit Euler updates for $x'=\alpha x$ with step $h=1/2$, initial state $x_0=1$, and scalar output $J=x_2$:
$$x_{k+1}=x_k+h\alpha x_k,\qquad k=0,1.$$
At $\alpha=1$, the tape has $x_1=3/2$ and $x_2=9/4$; reverse mode returns $dJ/d\alpha=3/2$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Substitution into the two Euler updates gives $x_1=1+(1/2)(1)(1)=3/2$ and $x_2=(3/2)+(1/2)(1)(3/2)=9/4$. As a function of $\alpha$, $J(\alpha)=(1+h\alpha)^2x_0$, so $J'(1)=2h(1+h)x_0=3/2$. [given, algebra]

Consider the real-arithmetic graph
$$z_1=x+y,\qquad z_2=z_1z_1,\qquad z_3=xy,\qquad f=z_2+z_3.$$
At $(x,y)=(1,2)$ it has output $f=11$. Both forward and reverse mode should give gradient $(8,7)$; the repeated parent slot in $z_2$ tests that its two edge contributions are both accumulated.

items.assessment: The Statement includes an empty generator list. The proof discards zero coefficients, uses the minimum of a finite nonempty list of positive ratios to reduce dependent support, and treats the empty independent support as the closed cone {0}. No constraint qualification is assumed here; singleton generators and zero vectors are covered by the same finite construction.

claim_sections.Statement:
For any finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n$, including the empty
list, the cone
$$
K=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m t_j a_j:t_j\ge0\right\}
$$
is a closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Every $y\in K$ has a representation whose positive-coefficient vectors are linearly independent. Start with any nonnegative coefficient list and discard its zero coefficients. If its remaining vectors are dependent, take a nonzero relation $\sum_j c_j a_j=0$ and change its sign so some $c_j>0$. For the current positive coefficients $t_j$, put $s=\min_{c_j>0}t_j/c_j$. Replacing each $t_j$ by $t_j-sc_j$ preserves the represented vector, leaves every coefficient nonnegative, and makes at least one positive coefficient zero. Repeating at most $m$ times leaves an independent positive support. [given, choose, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Every $y\in K$ has a representation whose positive-coefficient vectors are linearly independent. Start with any nonnegative coefficient list and discard its zero coefficients. If its remaining vectors are dependent, take a nonzero relation $\sum_j c_j a_j=0$ and change its sign so some $c_j>0$. For the current positive coefficients $t_j$, put $s=\min_{c_j>0}t_j/c_j$. Replacing each $t_j$ by $t_j-sc_j$ preserves the represented vector, leaves every coefficient nonnegative, and makes at least one positive coefficient zero. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix an independent index set $J$ and let $A_J$ have columns $a_j$, $j\in J$. Its Gram matrix $G_J=A_J^TA_J$ is invertible: for every nonzero $v$, $v^TG_Jv=\|A_Jv\|_2^2>0$ by independence. On the closed subspace $S_J=\operatorname{span}\{a_j:j\in J\}$, the map $R_J(y)=G_J^{-1}A_J^Ty$ is continuous and satisfies $A_JR_J(y)=y$. Hence $A_J(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})= S_J\cap R_J^{-1}(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})$ is closed: $S_J$ is closed by [F1], the nonnegative orthant is closed, and $R_J$ is continuous. For $J=\varnothing$ this cone is $\{0\}$, also closed. [given, F1, algebra]

items.assessment: The Statement requires a surjective derivative and a compatible second jet. The proof explicitly handles zero target dimension by the quadratic curve and otherwise uses the supplied regular-level graph and explicit correction z-v. A nonregular level is outside the hypothesis; a zero direction or acceleration remains a valid compatible jet, and no arbitrary family of curves is selected.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $H:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^2$, let $x\in U$, and
suppose $DH(x)$ is surjective. If $d\in\ker DH(x)$ and
$$DH(x)z+D^2H(x)[d,d]=0,$$
then there is a $C^2$ curve $\gamma$ on the level $H=H(x)$ near $0$ with
$\gamma(0)=x$, $\gamma'(0)=d$, and $\gamma''(0)=z$. For $q=0$ the level is
all of $U$ and the statement is immediate.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $q=0$, then $H$ is the unique map into $\mathbb R^0$ and the level is all of $U$. The curve $\gamma(t)=x+td+\tfrac12t^2z$ has the required value and first two derivatives. [given, construct]

Outside that cone it uses its unique nearest point and the explicit separating vector minus the projection residual; the final inner-product contradiction excludes simultaneous alternatives. It is an exactly-one alternative, not an iff whose two propositions are both true.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^r$. Exactly one of the
following holds:

1. There is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x\ge0$ and $Ax=b$.
2. There is $y\in\mathbb R^r$ with $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty<0$.

Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $r=0$, then $\mathbb R^r=\{0\}$ and $b=0$. Alternative 1 holds with $x=0\in\mathbb R^n$, while alternative 2 is impossible because the only $y\in\mathbb R^0$ is $0$ and $b^Ty=0$. This handles the zero-dimensional ambient case. Now assume $r\ge1$. Let $C=\{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j A_j:x_j\ge0\}$, where $A_j$ are the columns of $A$. This is a nonempty convex cone and is closed by [F1]. If $b\in C$, its nonnegative coefficients give alternative 1. If $b\notin C$, let $p$ be its nearest point in $C$ by [F2] and put $z=b-p\ne0$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

Alternative 1 holds with $x=0\in\mathbb R^n$, while alternative 2 is impossible because the only $y\in\mathbb R^0$ is $0$ and $b^Ty=0$. This handles the zero-dimensional ambient case. Now assume $r\ge1$. Let $C=\{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j A_j:x_j\ge0\}$, where $A_j$ are the columns of $A$. This is a nonempty convex cone and is closed by [F1]. If $b\in C$, its nonnegative coefficients give alternative 1. If $b\notin C$, let $p$ be its nearest point in $C$ by [F2] and put $z=b-p\ne0$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Applying [F3] with $c=0$ and $c=2p$ gives both $\langle z,p\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle z,p\rangle\le0$, hence $\langle z,p\rangle=0$. Applying [F3] to arbitrary $c\in C$ then gives $\langle z,c\rangle\le0$. In particular $A_j^Tz\le0$ for every column, and $\langle z,b\rangle=\langle z,p+z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Thus $y=-z$ satisfies $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty=-\|z\|_2^2<0$, which is alternative 2. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

items.assessment: The proof establishes both cone inclusions under MFCQ. With no active inequalities it sets w=0, and with no equalities it uses zero graph correction; otherwise a supplied MFCQ direction and regular-level graph produce an explicit feasible curve. Failure of MFCQ is outside this cone-equality claim, and finitely many active conditions share one sufficiently small positive time.

claim_sections.Statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], if MFCQ holds at a
feasible point $x$, then
$$T_C(x)=\mathcal L_C(x).$$

items.assessment: The Statement has a genuine equivalence: under KKT and a linearized direction, zero objective directional derivative is equivalent to zero derivatives on all positively weighted active constraints. The proof writes a finite sum of nonnegative terms; its vanishing forces each positive-weight term zero, and those zero terms conversely make the sum zero. Empty positive-weight index sets and zero directions remain covered.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $(x,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfy the KKT conditions for the program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For every
$d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$,
$$
\nabla f(x)^Td=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Dg_i(x)d=0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\text{ with }\lambda_i>0.
$$
Thus the critical cone is the linearized cone with equality imposed on each
positively weighted active inequality.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$, the equality term in stationarity vanishes, and inactive multipliers vanish by complementarity. Therefore $\nabla f(x)^Td=-\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_iDg_i(x)d$. Every summand on the right is nonnegative because $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $Dg_i(x)d\le0$. [given, F1, algebra]

Therefore $\nabla f(x)^Td=-\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_iDg_i(x)d$. Every summand on the right is nonnegative because $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $Dg_i(x)d\le0$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The sum in step 1.1 is zero exactly when each term with $\lambda_i>0$ is zero; because each such term is nonnegative, this is equivalent to $Dg_i(x)d=0$ for every positively weighted active index. Empty inequality/equality lists contribute zero to the Lagrangian. The proof takes infimum and supremum, not an attained optimizer or a choice of witnesses, and proves only the weak inequality.

claim_sections.Statement:
For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Since $x$ is feasible, $Ax-b=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$. Since $\lambda_i\ge0$, this gives $L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le f_0(x)$. The infimum defining $q$ is no larger than this particular Lagrangian value, so $q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)$. [given, F1, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The bound in step 1.1 holds for every primal feasible $x$ and every dual feasible pair. Taking the infimum over primal feasible $x$ and the supremum over dual feasible pairs gives $d^*\le p^*$ when the primal set is nonempty. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The proof treats the zero-dimensional affine hull with the zero functional. Otherwise it projects a specified sequence of points uniquely onto the nonempty epigraph closure and takes one convergent subsequence; a zero vertical support coefficient is excluded by the two-sided relative-interior ball. The positive vertical coefficient licenses division, with no claim at a missing relative-interior point.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let
$p:V\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, never $-\infty$, and finite somewhere.
If $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p)$ and $p(0)\in\mathbb R$, then
there is a linear functional $\ell:V\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$p(z)\ge p(0)+\ell(z)\qquad(z\in V).$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $W=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)$. Since $0$ belongs to the domain, $W$ is a linear subspace; relative interior gives a ball about $0$ in $W$ contained in $\operatorname{dom}p$. If $W=\{0\}$, take $\ell=0$. Otherwise identify $W$ with a Euclidean coordinate space. The restriction of $p$ to that open ball is finite and convex, so [F1] makes it continuous at $0$. [given, F1]

Since $0$ belongs to the domain, $W$ is a linear subspace; relative interior gives a ball about $0$ in $W$ contained in $\operatorname{dom}p$. If $W=\{0\}$, take $\ell=0$. Otherwise identify $W$ with a Euclidean coordinate space. The restriction of $p$ to that open ball is finite and convex, so [F1] makes it continuous at $0$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: In $W\times\mathbb R$, let $E=\{(z,t):p(z)\le t\}$ and let $\overline E$ be its closure. The set $E$ is convex, $(0,p(0))\in E$, and $\overline E$ is nonempty, closed and convex. Continuity from step 1.1 shows that $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)\notin\overline E$ for every $\epsilon>0$: choose $\delta>0$ so $p(z)>p(0)-\epsilon/3$ whenever $\|z\|<\delta$, while a sufficiently small open ball about $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)$ has $\|z\|<\delta$ and $t<p(0)-2\epsilon/3$, so it misses $E$. Thus $(0,p(0))$ is a boundary point of $\overline E$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

Since $(0,p(0))\in\overline E$, the projection distance is at most $1/k$, so $y_k\to(0,p(0))$. The unit vectors $a_k=(y_k-z_k)/\|y_k-z_k\|_2$ have a convergent subsequence by [F3], with unit limit $a=(s,\alpha)\in W\times\mathbb R$. If $\alpha=0$, points $(z,p(z))\in E$ for all sufficiently small $z$ and $-z$ in the ball from step 1.1 force both $\langle s,z\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle s,-z\rangle\ge0$. items.assessment: The Statement assumes a feasible local minimizer and MFCQ. The proof handles zero direction directly, then applies the finite Farkas alternative to paired equality columns and active inequalities, setting inactive multipliers zero explicitly. Existence uses one finite coefficient witness, not arbitrary simultaneous choices; multiplier uniqueness is not claimed here.

items.assessment: A feasible KKT tuple is given, so the comparison set contains the proposed minimizer. The proof separates zero from positive multipliers, applies convex gradient inequalities, and obtains the normal-cone inequality for every feasible point. It is a sufficient implication, does not require a nondegenerate active set, and introduces no arbitrary optimizer choice.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and suppose the objective
$f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities $g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable
and convex. Let the equalities be $Ax=b$. If a feasible tuple

items.assessment: The proof explicitly separates an empty critical unit set from a nonempty compact one. The former excludes all nearby bad points; the latter has a strictly positive minimum curvature and a finite-intersection contradiction. The zero critical cone is admitted and the condition is vacuous there; no constraint qualification is silently imposed.

claim_sections.Statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], suppose $x_*$ is
feasible and has KKT multipliers $(\nu,\lambda)$. If
$$
d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_*,\nu,\lambda)d>0\quad\text{for every nonzero }d\in\mathcal K(x_*,\nu,\lambda),
$$
then $x_*$ is a strict local minimizer. The condition is vacuous when the
critical cone is $\{0\}$; no constraint qualification is assumed.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Write $Q(d)=d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_*,\nu,\lambda)d$ and $S=\{d:\|d\|_2=1\}$. If this intersection is nonempty, it is compact by [F2], and [F2] gives a minimum $\gamma=\min Q(d)>0$ there. The relatively open set $N=\{u\in S:Q(u)>\gamma/2\}$ contains that intersection. If the intersection is empty, put $N=\varnothing$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

items.assessment: The Statement requires a finite attained primal value and relative-interior Slater point. The proof explicitly allows no inequalities by taking any positive eta and extends functionals only across finite bases; at the optimum every nonpositive complementarity term must vanish. Empty multiplier blocks and zero optimal multipliers are admissible, while failure of Slater/attainment is outside the conclusion.

claim_sections.Statement:
Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For perturbations $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and $v\in\mathbb R^p$, define $ P(u,v)=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le u_i\ (1\le i\le m),\ Ax-b=v\}. $ This value function is convex. Indeed, for two perturbations with finite values, choose feasible points with objective within $\epsilon$ of their respective infima. A convex combination of those points lies in $D$, its inequalities and equality residual are bounded by the same convex combination of perturbations, and convexity of $f_0$ bounds its objective. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the convex inequality. If one perturbation value is $-\infty$, arbitrarily low feasible objective values and the same convex-combination argument give value $-\infty$ at each strict convex combination with another feasible perturbation. [given, F1, construct]

Since the Slater point $x_s$ lies in every relative-interior domain, $x_s$ has a relative neighborhood in $S$ contained in $D$. Each $g_i$ is finite and convex on its domain and continuous near $x_s$ in its affine hull by [F4]; after intersecting finitely many neighborhoods, there are a relative neighborhood $U_s\subseteq D$ of $x_s$ and $\eta>0$ with $g_i(y)<-\eta$ on $U_s$ for every $i$ (take any $\eta>0$ if $m=0$). Thus $P(u,v)<+\infty$ on a relative neighborhood of $0$ in $Z=\mathbb R^m\times Y$. [given, F1, F4, construct]

claim_sections.Example:
Define the extended-real perspective

proper closed convex, the primal minimum is $1$, Slater fails, and the

items.assessment: The Definition requires positive finite state and noise dimensions. Its sums run over one through m and its scalar specialization sets both dimensions one; commutativity removes the antisymmetric contribution but noncommuting implementations require actual area information. It defines prescribed updates, not an iff theorem or arbitrary choice of a sampler.

claim_sections.Definition:
Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite integers, let $W=(W^1,\ldots,W^m)$ be the driving standard Brownian motion, and consider the autonomous It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\,dW^j_t,$$
where $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$. For a differentiable vector-valued function $f$, $Df(x)$ is its Jacobian and $L_i f(x):=Df(x)\sigma_i(x)$; this definition is applied componentwise when $f$ is matrix-valued.

On a deterministic grid $t_n=nh$, define $\Delta W_n^j=W^j_{t_{n+1}}-W^j_{t_n}$ and the iterated It\^o integral
$$I_{ij,n}:=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})\,dW^j_s,\qquad 1\le i,j\le m.$$
The integrand is predictable and square-integrable, so this is the $L^2$ It\^o integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]]; its finite energy is $\mathbb E\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}(W^i_s-W^i_{t_n})^2ds=h^2/2$ by [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]].

The general Milstein Taylor update is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}.$$
The diffusion fields have **commutative noise** when $L_i\sigma_j(x)=L_j\sigma_i(x)$ for every $x$ and every $i,j$. Under that condition, the equivalent update using only Brownian increments is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(Y_n)\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^m L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$
For scalar noise ($d=m=1$), this reads
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma(Y_n)\Delta W_n+\frac12\sigma(Y_n)\sigma'(Y_n)\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr).$$

For every $1\le i,j\le m$, define the Brownian area component $A_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}-I_{ji,n})/2$ and the symmetric part $S_{ij,n}:=(I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n})/2$. In particular, $A_{ii,n}=0$ and $S_{ii,n}=I_{ii,n}$. Then $A_{ji,n}=-A_{ij,n}$, $S_{ji,n}=S_{ij,n}$, and reindexing the sums gives
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j+L_j\sigma_i)S_{ij,n}+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j-L_j\sigma_i)A_{ij,n}.$$
The second sum vanishes under commutative noise; otherwise the general update includes the area components. A noncommuting Milstein implementation must sample or approximate the needed areas and account for their approximation error and computational cost; this definition makes no claim that an exact area sample is free or that a particular area sampler has a specified error rate.

For this pair, $C_b^k(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^q)$ means that every component and every partial derivative of orders at most $k$ exists, is continuous, and is bounded. This notation is componentwise for vector and matrix valued functions.

items.assessment: The imported noise dimension is positive and the step length strictly positive. Its proof pairs finitely many coordinate terms, including diagonal pairs, and derives the scalar conditional moments from the specified normal law. A zero area on diagonal is explicit; the resulting identities and commutative substitution are not biconditionals.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let the finite-dimensional Brownian It\^o setting and the integrals $I_{ij,n}$ be as in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]. For every grid interval of length $h>0$,
$$I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n}=\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h.$$
In the scalar case, writing $I_n=I_{11,n}$ and $\Delta W_n=\Delta W_n^1$, this gives
$$I_n=\frac12\bigl((\Delta W_n)^2-h\bigr),\quad \mathbb E[I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0,\quad \mathbb E[I_n^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=\frac{h^2}{2},\quad \mathbb E[\Delta W_n I_n\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]=0.$$
Consequently, under the commutativity condition in the Definition, the double-integral term in the general Milstein Taylor increment equals
$$\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)I_{ij,n}=\frac12\sum_{i,j}L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)\bigl(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h\bigr).$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F1] to $f(x)=x_i x_j$ on $[t_n,t_n+h]$. It gives $W^i_{t_n+h}W^j_{t_n+h}-W^i_{t_n}W^j_{t_n}=\int_{t_n}^{t_n+h}W_s^i\,dW_s^j+\int_{t_n}^{t_n+h}W_s^j\,dW_s^i+\delta_{ij}h$. Expand each integrand as its value at $t_n$ plus its Brownian increment; the two constant terms cancel from the two sides, leaving $\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j=I_{ij,n}+I_{ji,n}+\delta_{ij}h$. [F1, L1, A1]

items.assessment: The theorem assumes a positive deterministic interval and finite-energy predictable integrand; the event may be empty or null, giving zero weighted integrals. Its proof truncates elementary approximations to that interval and uses the declared AC-dependent Ito completion. It proves one weighted identity, not an iff or a new family-wide selection principle.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume AC and the Brownian filtration conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $t\ge0$, $h>0$, let $A\in\mathcal F_t$, and let $H$ be a real predictable process with finite energy on $[t,t+h]$ and $H_s=0$ for $s\notin(t,t+h]$. For any coordinate $W^j$ of the driving finite-dimensional Brownian motion,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A\left|\int_t^{t+h}H_s\,dW_s^j\right|^2\right]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A\int_t^{t+h}|H_s|^2\,ds\right].$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Choose elementary predictable $H^n\to H$ in $L^2(ds\,dP)$ using [F4], and replace each $H^n$ by $\widetilde H^n=\mathbf1_{(t,t+h]}H^n$. Refining its finite partition at $t$ and $t+h$ makes $\widetilde H^n$ elementary; because $H$ vanishes off this interval, $\widetilde H^n\to H$ in $L^2(ds\,dP)$. [F2, F4, given]

Refining its finite partition at $t$ and $t+h$ makes $\widetilde H^n$ elementary; because $H$ vanishes off this interval, $\widetilde H^n\to H$ in $L^2(ds\,dP)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Refine the partition of $\widetilde H^n$ so that every nonzero cell $(s_k,s_{k+1}]$ has $s_k\ge t$. Thus $\mathbf1_A\widetilde H^n$ is elementary predictable for the Brownian coordinate in [F1], and the finite-sum definition [F3] gives $\int\mathbf1_A\widetilde H^n dW^j=\mathbf1_A\int\widetilde H^n dW^j$. Applying [F5] to $\mathbf1_A\widetilde H^n$ yields $$\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A\left|\int\widetilde H^n dW^j\right|^2\right]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A\int|\widetilde H^n|^2ds\right].$$ [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $X$ solve the autonomous SDE in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]] on a filtered probability space with an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the filtration. Assume $b,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in C_b^3(\mathbb R^d)$, with the $C_b^3$ convention of the Definition. There is a constant $C$ depending only on the coefficient bounds and $d,m$ such that for every $t\ge0$, $0\le r\le1$, and $A\in\mathcal F_t$,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A|X_{t+r}-X_t|^2\right]\le Cr\,P(A),\qquad \mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A|X_{t+r}-X_t|^4\right]\le Cr^2\,P(A).$$
These event-weighted inequalities are the conditional second- and fourth-moment bounds for the increment.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Put $Y_s=X_s-X_t$, and let $B$ bound $|b|$ and $S^2$ bound $\sum_j|\sigma_j|^2$. The integral equation, $|\int_t^{t+r}b(X_s)ds|^2\le B^2r^2$, the finite-sum inequality $|\sum_jv_j|^2\le m\sum_j|v_j|^2$, and [F2] give $$\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|Y_{t+r}|^2]\le2B^2r^2P(A)+2S^2rP(A)\le C rP(A),$$ since $r\le1$. The event-weighted identity applies to each integrand $\sigma_j(X_s)\mathbf1_{(t,t+r]}(s)$, whose squared norm is bounded by $\|\sigma_j\|_\infty^2$. [L1, F1, F2, A1]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Put $Y_s=X_s-X_t$, and let $B$ bound $|b|$ and $S^2$ bound $\sum_j|\sigma_j|^2$. The integral equation, $|\int_t^{t+r}b(X_s)ds|^2\le B^2r^2$, the finite-sum inequality $|\sum_jv_j|^2\le m\sum_j|v_j|^2$, and [F2] give $$\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|Y_{t+r}|^2]\le2B^2r^2P(A)+2S^2rP(A)\le C rP(A),$$ since $r\le1$. The event-weighted identity applies to each integrand $\sigma_j(X_s)\mathbf1_{(t,t+r]}(s)$, whose squared norm is bounded by $\|\sigma_j\|_\infty^2$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $R>0$, use the continuous adapted version from [F1], modifying it on its exceptional null set if necessary; usual completeness makes this an adapted null modification and leaves all moment and SDE assertions unchanged. Let $\theta_R=\inf\{u\ge0:|Y_{t+u}|\ge R\}$. This is a stopping time: for fixed $u$, $\{\theta_R\le u\}=\{\sup_{0\le v\le u}|Y_{t+v}|\ge R\}$, and continuity makes the supremum equal to the supremum over rational $v\in[0,u]$ together with $u$, hence $\mathcal F_{t+u}$-measurable. Put $Y^R_u=X_{t+(u\wedge\theta_R)}-X_t=Y_{t+(u\wedge\theta_R)}$, $q_R(u)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|Y^R_u|^4]$, and $p_R(u)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|Y^R_u|^2]$. By the stopped representation in [F1], the drift and diffusion integrands are multiplied by $\mathbf1_{s-t\le\theta_R}$. Its drift square is at most $B^2u^2$, and applying [F2] coordinatewise with the finite-sum bound gives $p_R(u)\le2B^2u^2P(A)+2S^2uP(A)\le C uP(A)$, by the same bound as step 1.1. Apply [F3] to $f(y)=|y|^4$ and the stopped process. The Hessian formula gives drift $4|Y^R|^2\langle Y^R,b(X)\rangle+2|Y^R|^2\sum_j|\sigma_j(X)|^2+4\sum_j\langle Y^R,\sigma_j(X)\rangle^2$ before the stopping time. Bounded coefficients and $4B|Y^R|^3\le C(|Y^R|^4+|Y^R|^2)$ bound its absolute value by $C(|Y^R|^4+|Y^R|^2)$. The stopped stochastic integrand is bounded, so [F4] makes its expectation after multiplication by $\mathbf1_A$ zero. Consequently $$q_R(u)\le C\int_0^u q_R(v)\,dv+C u^2P(A),\qquad 0\le u\le r.$$ The second term follows from $p_R(v)\le CvP(A)$; all constants are independent of $R$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

By the stopped representation in [F1], the drift and diffusion integrands are multiplied by $\mathbf1_{s-t\le\theta_R}$. Its drift square is at most $B^2u^2$, and applying [F2] coordinatewise with the finite-sum bound gives $p_R(u)\le2B^2u^2P(A)+2S^2uP(A)\le C uP(A)$, by the same bound as step 1.1. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Define $Q_R(u)=\int_0^u q_R(v)\,dv$. The inequality in step 2.1 implies $Q_R'(u)\le C Q_R(u)+C u^2P(A)$ for almost every $u$, with $Q_R(0)=0$. Multiplying by $e^{-Cu}$ and integrating gives $Q_R(u)\le C' u^3P(A)$ for $u\le1$. Returning to step 2.1 gives $q_R(u)\le C''u^2P(A)$. claim_sections.Statement:
Let $X$ solve the finite-dimensional autonomous SDE in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]] with $b,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in C_b^3(\mathbb R^d)$, using the $C_b^3$ convention in that Definition. Let $0<h\le1$ and let $[t,t+h]$ be a deterministic interval. Define $L_0f:=Df\,b+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^mD^2f[\sigma_k,\sigma_k]$ and $L_if:=Df\,\sigma_i$ for $i\ge1$. Then there is a remainder $R_{t,h}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$X_{t+h}=X_t+b(X_t)h+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)\Delta W^j+\sum_{i,j=1}^mL_i\sigma_j(X_t)I_{ij}+R_{t,h},$$
where $\Delta W^j=W^j_{t+h}-W^j_t$ and $I_{ij}=\int_t^{t+h}(W_s^i-W_t^i)dW_s^j$. Moreover, for the conditioning sigma algebra $\mathcal F_t$ there is a conditional-expectation version $r_{t,h}=\mathbb E[R_{t,h}\mid\mathcal F_t]$ with
$$|r_{t,h}|\le Ch^2,\qquad \mathbb E[|R_{t,h}|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le Ch^3\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,m$ and the coefficient bounds, not on $t,h$ or $X_t$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F2] to $f=\sigma_j$ on $[t,s]$. With the operators in [L1], $$\sigma_j(X_s)=\sigma_j(X_t)+\int_t^s(L_0\sigma_j)(X_r)dr+\sum_i\int_t^s(L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)dW_r^i.$$ Integrating this identity against $dW_s^j$, summing over $j$, and substituting the SDE decomposition of $X_{t+h}-X_t$ isolates the constant coefficient terms. Thus the remainder is exactly $$R_{t,h}=R_b+R_0+R_1,$$ where $R_b=\int_t^{t+h}(b(X_s)-b(X_t))ds$, $R_0=\sum_j\int_t^{t+h}(\int_t^s(L_0\sigma_j)(X_r)dr)dW_s^j$, and $R_1=\sum_{i,j}\int_t^{t+h}(\int_t^s((L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)-(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t))dW_r^i)dW_s^j$. The subtraction in $R_1$ leaves precisely $\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t)I_{ij}$. [L1, F1, F2, A1]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Apply [F2] to $f=\sigma_j$ on $[t,s]$. With the operators in [L1], $$\sigma_j(X_s)=\sigma_j(X_t)+\int_t^s(L_0\sigma_j)(X_r)dr+\sum_i\int_t^s(L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)dW_r^i.$$ Integrating this identity against $dW_s^j$, summing over $j$, and substituting the SDE decomposition of $X_{t+h}-X_t$ isolates the constant coefficient terms. Thus the remainder is exactly $$R_{t,h}=R_b+R_0+R_1,$$ where $R_b=\int_t^{t+h}(b(X_s)-b(X_t))ds$, $R_0=\sum_j\int_t^{t+h}(\int_t^s(L_0\sigma_j)(X_r)dr)dW_s^j$, and $R_1=\sum_{i,j}\int_t^{t+h}(\int_t^s((L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)-(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t))dW_r^i)dW_s^j$. The subtraction in $R_1$ leaves precisely $\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t)I_{ij}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Since $L_0b$ is bounded, apply [F2] to $b(X_s)$ and take event integrals over $A\in\mathcal F_t$. The stochastic increments have zero event integral by [F4]; componentwise this gives $|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_b]|\le\|L_0b\|_\infty h^2P(A)/2$. By [F5]--[F6], the vector conditional expectation $r_b=\mathbb E[R_b\mid\mathcal F_t]$, formed coordinatewise, exists. If any coordinate exceeded its bound on an $\mathcal F_t$ event, the defining event-integral identity [F5] would contradict the bound just proved, so $|r_b|\le Ch^2$ after increasing $C$ by a dimension factor. Also, the pathwise inequality $|\int_t^{t+h}g(s)ds|^2\le h\int_t^{t+h}|g(s)|^2ds$ follows by applying $0\le\int_t^{t+h}(|g|-a)^2ds$ with $a=h^{-1}\int_t^{t+h}|g|ds$; [L2] therefore gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|R_b|^2]\le h\|Db\|_\infty^2\int_t^{t+h}C(s-t)P(A)ds\le Ch^3P(A)$. [L2, F2, F4, F5, F6, A1]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Since $L_0b$ is bounded, apply [F2] to $b(X_s)$ and take event integrals over $A\in\mathcal F_t$. The stochastic increments have zero event integral by [F4]; componentwise this gives $|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_b]|\le\|L_0b\|_\infty h^2P(A)/2$. By [F5]--[F6], the vector conditional expectation $r_b=\mathbb E[R_b\mid\mathcal F_t]$, formed coordinatewise, exists. Also, the pathwise inequality $|\int_t^{t+h}g(s)ds|^2\le h\int_t^{t+h}|g(s)|^2ds$ follows by applying $0\le\int_t^{t+h}(|g|-a)^2ds$ with $a=h^{-1}\int_t^{t+h}|g|ds$; [L2] therefore gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|R_b|^2]\le h\|Db\|_\infty^2\int_t^{t+h}C(s-t)P(A)ds\le Ch^3P(A)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Each $L_0\sigma_j$ is bounded. Therefore the inner integral in $R_0$ has magnitude at most $C(s-t)$. Its outer It\^o integrals have zero conditional mean by [F4]. Apply the scalar event-weighted identity [F3] to each component of each outer vector integral and use $|\sum_jv_j|^2\le m\sum_j|v_j|^2$; this gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|R_0|^2]\le C\int_t^{t+h}(s-t)^2ds\,P(A)\le Ch^3P(A)$. [F3, F4, A1]

Apply the scalar event-weighted identity [F3] to each component of each outer vector integral and use $|\sum_jv_j|^2\le m\sum_j|v_j|^2$; this gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|R_0|^2]\le C\int_t^{t+h}(s-t)^2ds\,P(A)\le Ch^3P(A)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Each $L_i\sigma_j$ is globally Lipschitz: its derivative is a sum of products of first and second derivatives of the $\sigma_k$, bounded by [L1]. The inner integral $J_{ij}(s)=\int_t^s((L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)-(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t))dW_r^i$ has zero conditional mean and, by [F3] coordinatewise and [L2], satisfies $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|J_{ij}(s)|^2]\le C\int_t^s\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|X_r-X_t|^2]dr\le C(s-t)^2P(A)$. Each outer integral has zero conditional mean by [F4]; applying the scalar identity [F3] componentwise and $|\sum_{ij}v_{ij}|^2\le m^2\sum_{ij}|v_{ij}|^2$ gives $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|R_1|^2]\le Ch^3P(A)$. The inner integral $J_{ij}(s)=\int_t^s((L_i\sigma_j)(X_r)-(L_i\sigma_j)(X_t))dW_r^i$ has zero conditional mean and, by [F3] coordinatewise and [L2], satisfies $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|J_{ij}(s)|^2]\le C\int_t^s\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A|X_r-X_t|^2]dr\le C(s-t)^2P(A)$. claim_sections.Statement:
Let $N\ge1$, $0<h\le1$, and $Nh\le T$. Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n=0}^N$ be a filtration as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. For every $n$, let $e_n,u_n,r_n$ be square-integrable $\mathbb R^d$-valued, $\mathcal F_n$-measurable random vectors; let $M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}$ be square-integrable and $\mathcal F_{n+1}$-measurable. Say $Z$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal F_n$ if $\mathbb E\langle H,Z\rangle=0$ for every square-integrable $\mathcal F_n$-measurable vector $H$. Suppose
$$e_0=0,\quad e_{n+1}=e_n+hu_n+r_n+M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1},$$
$$|u_n|\le L|e_n|,\qquad |r_n|\le C_0h^2,$$
and $M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}$ are orthogonal to $\mathcal F_n$, with
$$\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2\le C_1h\,\mathbb E|e_n|^2,\qquad \mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2\le C_1h^3.$$
Then $\mathbb E|e_N|^2\le C_T h^2$, where $C_T$ depends only on $T,L,C_0,C_1$ and not on $h$ or $N$. This is a local-to-global estimate for an order-one grid RMS error when the drift error is Lipschitz and the centered one-step defect has second moment $O(h^3)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Since $|e_n+hu_n|\le(1+Lh)|e_n|$ and $|r_n|\le C_0h^2$, the elementary inequality $2ab\le h a^2+h^{-1}b^2$ and $h\le1$ give $$\mathbb E|e_n+hu_n+r_n|^2\le(1+C h)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$ Indeed, the square of $e_n+hu_n$ contributes at most $(1+Lh)^2|e_n|^2\le(1+C h)|e_n|^2$, its cross term with $r_n$ is bounded by $C h^2|e_n|\le C h|e_n|^2+C h^3$, and $|r_n|^2\le C h^4\le C h^3$. [given, F1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Since $|e_n+hu_n|\le(1+Lh)|e_n|$ and $|r_n|\le C_0h^2$, the elementary inequality $2ab\le h a^2+h^{-1}b^2$ and $h\le1$ give $$\mathbb E|e_n+hu_n+r_n|^2\le(1+C h)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$ Indeed, the square of $e_n+hu_n$ contributes at most $(1+Lh)^2|e_n|^2\le(1+C h)|e_n|^2$, its cross term with $r_n$ is bounded by $C h^2|e_n|\le C h|e_n|^2+C h^3$, and $|r_n|^2\le C h^4\le C h^3$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Orthogonality makes the cross expectation between $e_n+hu_n+r_n$ and $M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1}$ zero. To bound the remaining cross term, put $a=|M_{n+1}|$ and $b=|Q_{n+1}|$; nonnegativity of $\mathbb E(a-\lambda b)^2$ for every real $\lambda$ implies $\mathbb E[ab]\le(\mathbb Ea^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb Eb^2)^{1/2}$. Hence $$2|\mathbb E\langle M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}\rangle|\le2(\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2)^{1/2}\le C h^2(\mathbb E|e_n|^2)^{1/2}\le C h\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$ The final inequality is $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ with factors proportional to $h^{1/2}(\mathbb E|e_n|^2)^{1/2}$ and $h^{3/2}$. Therefore the recurrence and step 1.1 imply $$\mathbb E|e_{n+1}|^2\le(1+C h)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$ [given, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Orthogonality makes the cross expectation between $e_n+hu_n+r_n$ and $M_{n+1}+Q_{n+1}$ zero. To bound the remaining cross term, put $a=|M_{n+1}|$ and $b=|Q_{n+1}|$; nonnegativity of $\mathbb E(a-\lambda b)^2$ for every real $\lambda$ implies $\mathbb E[ab]\le(\mathbb Ea^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb Eb^2)^{1/2}$. Hence $$2|\mathbb E\langle M_{n+1},Q_{n+1}\rangle|\le2(\mathbb E|M_{n+1}|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|Q_{n+1}|^2)^{1/2}\le C h^2(\mathbb E|e_n|^2)^{1/2}\le C h\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$ The final inequality is $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ with factors proportional to $h^{1/2}(\mathbb E|e_n|^2)^{1/2}$ and $h^{3/2}$. Therefore the recurrence and step 1.1 imply $$\mathbb E|e_{n+1}|^2\le(1+C h)\mathbb E|e_n|^2+C h^3.$$

items.assessment: The Statement fixes positive finite state/noise dimensions, positive horizon and positive grid count. Its proof explicitly treats scalar noise as automatically commutative and zero diffusion as the deterministic recurrence; the grid maximum includes both time endpoints. AC stays in the Brownian/Ito suppliers, and the rate is conditional rather than biconditional.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, let $W$ be an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a filtration satisfying [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], and let $X$ solve
$$dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(X_t)dW_t^j,\qquad X_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^d).$$
Assume $b,\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\in C_b^3(\mathbb R^d)$ as defined in [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]. Put $L_i f=Df\,\sigma_i$ and assume commutative noise $L_i\sigma_j=L_j\sigma_i$ for all $i,j$. On the uniform grid $t_n=nh$, $h=T/N\le1$, initialize $Y_0=X_0$ and use the product-increment Milstein update in the Definition. Then there is a constant $C_T$, independent of $N$, such that
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\mathbb E|Y_n-X_{t_n}|^2\le C_T h^2.$$
Thus the grid root-mean-square error is $O(h)$ on $[0,T]$. For $m=1$ the commutativity condition is automatic and the scheme is the scalar Milstein update. No claim is made for a noncommuting-noise scheme without an area sampler satisfying a separately proved approximation bound.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Define $e_n=Y_n-X_{t_n}$. Apply [L3] to the exact solution on $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Using [L2] and commutativity, the exact Taylor increment has the same product form as the update [L1], except that its coefficients are evaluated at $X_{t_n}$ and it includes the remainder $R_{n+1}$. [F1, L1, L2, L3, given]

Using [L2] and commutativity, the exact Taylor increment has the same product form as the update [L1], except that its coefficients are evaluated at $X_{t_n}$ and it includes the remainder $R_{n+1}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text:
Subtract the exact update from [L1]. With $u_n=b(Y_n)-b(X_{t_n})$, set
$$M_{n+1}=\sum_j(\sigma_j(Y_n)-\sigma_j(X_{t_n}))\Delta W_n^j+\frac12\sum_{i,j}(L_i\sigma_j(Y_n)-L_i\sigma_j(X_{t_n}))(\Delta W_n^i\Delta W_n^j-\delta_{ij}h).$$
Then $e_{n+1}=e_n+hu_n+M_{n+1}-R_{n+1}$. The increments after $t_n$ are independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ by [F1]; their first moments vanish, and each centered quadratic factor has mean zero. Hence $M_{n+1}$ is orthogonal to every square-integrable $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable vector. [F1, L1, L3, step 1.1]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The derivatives of $b$ are bounded, so $|u_n|\le C|e_n|$. Also each $L_i\sigma_j$ is globally Lipschitz: its derivative is a sum of products of first and second derivatives of the diffusion fields, all bounded by [L1]. The linear Gaussian term in $M_{n+1}$ has conditional second moment at most $Ch|e_n|^2$. For the quadratic term, $\mathbb E[(\Delta W_i\Delta W_j-\delta_{ij}h)^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}]\le2h^2$ by independent centered normal coordinates; the finite sum and the Lipschitz bound therefore give second moment at most $Ch^2|e_n|^2\le Ch|e_n|^2$. items.assessment: The Definition fixes a scalar state, one positive time step and one shared normal increment for predictor/corrector. A zero constant diffusion is admitted and removes the stochastic additions. This is a prescribed two-stage map under declared Brownian AC assumptions, not an assertion of a weak-order equivalence for multiplicative noise.

claim_sections.Definition:
Assume AC and the Brownian filtered-space conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Consider the scalar additive-noise It\^o SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t,$$
where $\sigma\in\mathbb R$ is constant. Given a step size $h>0$, a grid value $Y_n$, and the Brownian increment $\Delta W_n=W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}$, the explicit stochastic Heun update is the two-stage rule
$$Z_n=Y_n+b(Y_n)h+\sigma\Delta W_n,\qquad Y_{n+1}=Y_n+\frac h2\bigl(b(Y_n)+b(Z_n)\bigr)+\sigma\Delta W_n.$$
The predictor $Z_n$ uses the same increment as the corrector. One step evaluates $b$ at $Y_n$ and $Z_n$ and uses one Gaussian increment. The weak order-two guarantee authored in this pair is only for this constant-diffusion scheme; the displayed update omits terms required for the corresponding multiplicative-noise guarantee.

In this definition and its consumers, $C_b^k(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$ means that the function and all its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded.

items.assessment: The theorem assumes 0<h<=1, a scalar Gaussian increment and the bounded classical backward solution. Its proof lists finitely many Gaussian moments, including zero odd moments, and cancels matching terms through second order. Positive step/one-dimensional state exclude an empty scheme instance, and the local weak bound is not an iff.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $b\in C_b^6(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, let $\sigma\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and define the generator $Lf=b f'+\frac12\sigma^2f''$. Let $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $u_t+Lu=0$. Assume all mixed derivatives $\partial_t^r\partial_x^j u$ for $0\le r\le3$ and $0\le j\le6$ are continuous and bounded. For $0<h\le1$, $t+h\le T$, fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, and $w\sim N(0,h)$, take one Heun step from [[def-additive-noise-stochastic-heun-scheme]] and let $D=Y_{n+1}-x$. Then a constant $C$, uniform in $t,x,h$, satisfies
$$\left|\mathbb E\bigl[u(t+h,x+D)\bigr]-u(t,x)\right|\le Ch^3.$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Put $B=b(x)$, $B_j=b^{(j)}(x)$, $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$, and $D=\sigma w+Bh+\frac h2(b(x+\delta)-B)$. Taylor's formula through degree three gives $b(x+\delta)=B+B_1\delta+\frac12B_2\delta^2+\frac16B_3\delta^3+\rho_4$, with $|\rho_4|\le\|b^{(4)}\|_\infty|\delta|^4/24$. From [F1], $\mathbb Ew=0$, $\mathbb Ew^2=h$, $\mathbb Ew^3=0$, $\mathbb Ew^4=3h^2$, $\mathbb Ew^5=0$, and $\mathbb E|w|^6=15h^3$. Substituting $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$ and collecting terms of order at most $h^2$ gives $$\begin{aligned}\mathbb ED&=Bh+\left(\frac12BB_1+\frac14\sigma^2B_2\right)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^2&=\sigma^2h+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^3&=3B\sigma^2h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^4&=3\sigma^4h^2+O(h^3),\qquad \mathbb ED^5=O(h^3).\end{aligned}$$ For the second moment, the $h^2$ terms are $(Bh)^2$ and $2(\sigma w)(\frac12B_1\sigma hw)$; for the third they are $3(\sigma w)^2(Bh)$; for the fourth it is $\mathbb E(\sigma w)^4$. All other terms either contain an odd Gaussian moment or have expected magnitude $O(h^3)$ by $\mathbb E|\delta|^4=O(h^2)$ and the displayed remainder bound. Since $b$ is bounded, $|D|\le |\sigma||w|+h\|b\|_\infty$, so $\mathbb E|D|^6\le Ch^3$. [L1, F1, A1]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Put $B=b(x)$, $B_j=b^{(j)}(x)$, $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$, and $D=\sigma w+Bh+\frac h2(b(x+\delta)-B)$. Taylor's formula through degree three gives $b(x+\delta)=B+B_1\delta+\frac12B_2\delta^2+\frac16B_3\delta^3+\rho_4$, with $|\rho_4|\le\|b^{(4)}\|_\infty|\delta|^4/24$. From [F1], $\mathbb Ew=0$, $\mathbb Ew^2=h$, $\mathbb Ew^3=0$, $\mathbb Ew^4=3h^2$, $\mathbb Ew^5=0$, and $\mathbb E|w|^6=15h^3$. Substituting $\delta=Bh+\sigma w$ and collecting terms of order at most $h^2$ gives $$\begin{aligned}\mathbb ED&=Bh+\left(\frac12BB_1+\frac14\sigma^2B_2\right)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^2&=\sigma^2h+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^3&=3B\sigma^2h^2+O(h^3),\\\mathbb ED^4&=3\sigma^4h^2+O(h^3),\qquad \mathbb ED^5=O(h^3).\end{aligned}$$ For the second moment, the $h^2$ terms are $(Bh)^2$ and $2(\sigma w)(\frac12B_1\sigma hw)$; for the third they are $3(\sigma w)^2(Bh)$; for the fourth it is $\mathbb E(\sigma w)^4$. All other terms either contain an odd Gaussian moment or have expected magnitude $O(h^3)$ by $\mathbb E|\delta|^4=O(h^2)$ and the displayed remainder bound. Since $b$ is bounded, $|D|\le |\sigma||w|+h\|b\|_\infty$, so $\mathbb E|D|^6\le Ch^3$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Taylor-expand $u(t+h,x+D)$ in its spatial argument through degree five. The sixth-derivative bound and step 1.1 yield $$\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u+u_x\mathbb ED+\frac12u_{xx}\mathbb ED^2+\frac16u_{xxx}\mathbb ED^3+\frac1{24}u_{xxxx}\mathbb ED^4+\frac1{120}u_{xxxxx}\mathbb ED^5+O(h^3),$$ where the displayed derivatives are evaluated at $(t+h,x)$. Substituting the moment formulas, the coefficients through order $h^2$ are $hLu$ and $\frac12h^2L^2u$, because $$L^2u=\left(BB_1+\frac12\sigma^2B_2\right)u_x+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)u_{xx}+B\sigma^2u_{xxx}+\frac14\sigma^4u_{xxxx}.$$ Thus $\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3)$. [L1, F1, step 1.1]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Taylor-expand $u(t+h,x+D)$ in its spatial argument through degree five. The sixth-derivative bound and step 1.1 yield $$\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u+u_x\mathbb ED+\frac12u_{xx}\mathbb ED^2+\frac16u_{xxx}\mathbb ED^3+\frac1{24}u_{xxxx}\mathbb ED^4+\frac1{120}u_{xxxxx}\mathbb ED^5+O(h^3),$$ where the displayed derivatives are evaluated at $(t+h,x)$. Substituting the moment formulas, the coefficients through order $h^2$ are $hLu$ and $\frac12h^2L^2u$, because $$L^2u=\left(BB_1+\frac12\sigma^2B_2\right)u_x+(B^2+\sigma^2B_1)u_{xx}+B\sigma^2u_{xxx}+\frac14\sigma^4u_{xxxx}.$$ Thus $\mathbb E u(t+h,x+D)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Since $u_t=-Lu$ and $L$ is independent of $t$, differentiating the backward equation gives $u_{tt}=L^2u$. Taylor's formula in time at fixed $x$, with bounded $u_{ttt}$, therefore gives $$u(t,x)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3).$$ The coefficient and derivative bounds in the Statement make the constants in the preceding expansions uniform in $t,x,h$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

Taylor's formula in time at fixed $x$, with bounded $u_{ttt}$, therefore gives $$u(t,x)=u(t+h,x)+hLu(t+h,x)+\frac12h^2L^2u(t+h,x)+O(h^3).$$ The coefficient and derivative bounds in the Statement make the constants in the preceding expansions uniform in $t,x,h$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The expansions in steps 2.1 and 3.1 have identical terms through order $h^2$; subtracting them leaves a remainder bounded by $Ch^3$, which is the asserted one-step weak defect. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.assessment: The theorem fixes a scalar additive-noise SDE, deterministic initial value and a positive uniform grid with Nh=T. The proof telescopes the stated one-step backward-solution errors and substitutes the terminal payoff; it does not infer multiplicative-noise order or existence of an arbitrary payoff's backward solution. Its rate claim is one-way.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume AC and the Brownian filtration conventions in [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Consider $dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sigma dW_t$ on $[0,T]$, where $b\in C_b^6(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, $\sigma\in\mathbb R$ is constant, and $X_0=x_0\in\mathbb R$ is deterministic. For $t\le T$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, let $X^{t,x}$ denote the solution of the same SDE started from $x$ at time $t$. Let $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ have a bounded classical backward solution $u(t,x)=\mathbb E[\phi(X_T^{t,x})]$ with $u(T,x)=\phi(x)$, $u_t+Lu=0$, $L=b\partial_x+\frac12\sigma^2\partial_{xx}$, and all mixed derivatives $\partial_t^r\partial_x^j u$ for $0\le r\le3$ and $0\le j\le6$ continuous and bounded. On a uniform grid $h=T/N\le1$, initialize $Y_0=x_0$ and apply the additive-noise stochastic Heun update in [[def-additive-noise-stochastic-heun-scheme]]. There is a constant $C_T$, independent of $h$, such that
$$\left|\mathbb E\phi(Y_N)-\mathbb E\phi(X_T)\right|\le C_T h^2.$$
This is weak order two, meaning the expectation error is bounded by a constant times $h^2$ for the stated payoff class. The claim is specific to constant additive diffusion; no multiplicative-noise order-two result is asserted.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For each $n$, the numerical value $Y_n$ is $\mathcal F_{t_n}$-measurable by induction from the update [L1]. The next increment $\Delta W_n$ is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ by [F1]. Therefore the joint law of $(Y_n,\Delta W_n)$ is the product of the law of $Y_n$ and $N(0,h)$; integrating the uniform one-step bound [L2] against the law of $Y_n$ gives $$\left|\mathbb E u(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})-\mathbb E u(t_n,Y_n)\right|\le Ch^3.$$ [F1, L1, L2, given]

The next increment $\Delta W_n$ is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ by [F1]. Therefore the joint law of $(Y_n,\Delta W_n)$ is the product of the law of $Y_n$ and $N(0,h)$; integrating the uniform one-step bound [L2] against the law of $Y_n$ gives $$\left|\mathbb E u(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})-\mathbb E u(t_n,Y_n)\right|\le Ch^3.$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Sum the inequalities in step 1.1 over $n=0,\ldots,N-1$. The intermediate expectations telescope, so $$\left|\mathbb E u(T,Y_N)-\mathbb E u(0,Y_0)\right|\le NCh^3=C_T h^2,$$ because $Nh=T$. [step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Sum the inequalities in step 1.1 over $n=0,\ldots,N-1$. The intermediate expectations telescope, so $$\left|\mathbb E u(T,Y_N)-\mathbb E u(0,Y_0)\right|\le NCh^3=C_T h^2,$$ because $Nh=T$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The terminal condition gives $u(T,Y_N)=\phi(Y_N)$. Since $Y_0=x_0$ and $u(0,x_0)$ is the expectation of $\phi$ for the exact SDE started at $(0,x_0)$, $\mathbb E u(0,Y_0)=u(0,x_0)=\mathbb E\phi(X_T)$. Substituting these identities into step 2.1 yields the claimed weak error. The argument uses only the admitted additive-noise backward solution and makes no inference for state-dependent diffusion. [A1, step 2.1, given] ∎
