items.assessment: The theorem has positive finite dimensions and horizon and a nonempty dyadic hierarchy starting at level zero. Its proof handles that base level separately for variance and absorbs finitely many coarser grids, then uses nested coupling for the rate exponents. No iff or arbitrary area-sampler selection is claimed; the commutative fixed-cost hypotheses remain explicit.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume AC and the scalar or commutative-noise SDE hypotheses of [[thm-commutative-milstein-strong-order-one]]. Let $T>0$, use dyadic step sizes $h_\ell=T2^{-\ell}$, and let $\psi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Lipschitz. At each level form the Milstein approximation $Y_\ell(T)$; couple adjacent levels by using the same Brownian path, so each coarse increment is the sum of its two fine increments. Put $P_\ell=\psi(Y_\ell(T))$ and let $\Delta_\ell=P_\ell^f-P_{\ell-1}^c$ for $\ell\ge1$, as in [[def-mlmc-hierarchy-and-coupled-corrections]]. For fixed finite $d,m$ and bounded-cost coefficient and derivative evaluations, constants independent of $\ell$ satisfy
$$|\mathbb E P_\ell-\mathbb E\psi(X_T)|\le C_bh_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\Delta_\ell)\le C_vh_\ell^2,\qquad C_\ell\le C_ch_\ell^{-1}.$$
The exact statement and proof of [[thm-mlmc-complexity-under-rate-assumptions]] then give an MLMC estimator with root-mean-square error at most $\epsilon$ and total work $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$. The variance statement is for Lipschitz terminal payoffs and the stated nested coupling; no Euler correction-rate theorem or area-sampling cost is substituted.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For all sufficiently fine levels, [L2] gives $\|Y_\ell(T)-X_T\|_2\le C h_\ell$, where $\|Z\|_2=(\mathbb E|Z|^2)^{1/2}$. There are only finitely many coarser dyadic levels; each has finitely many steps and finite second moments because the coefficients and derivatives are bounded. Enlarging $C$ therefore makes the same error bound valid for every level. The same argument gives $\mathbb E|\psi(Y_\ell(T))|^2<\infty$, since $|\psi(x)|\le |\psi(0)|+\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)|x|$. [L1, L2, given]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For all sufficiently fine levels, [L2] gives $\|Y_\ell(T)-X_T\|_2\le C h_\ell$, where $\|Z\|_2=(\mathbb E|Z|^2)^{1/2}$. There are only finitely many coarser dyadic levels; each has finitely many steps and finite second moments because the coefficients and derivatives are bounded. Enlarging $C$ therefore makes the same error bound valid for every level. The same argument gives $\mathbb E|\psi(Y_\ell(T))|^2<\infty$, since $|\psi(x)|\le |\psi(0)|+\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)|x|$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: A level-$\ell$ fine path has $T/h_\ell=2^\ell$ steps and its coarse companion has $2^{\ell-1}$ steps. Each commutative Milstein step uses a fixed finite number of coefficient/derivative evaluations and Gaussian vector samples for fixed $d,m$; [L1] requires no Lévy-area sampler. Thus one correction sample has work at most $C(2^\ell+2^{\ell-1})\le C_ch_\ell^{-1}$, including the finitely many coarse initial levels after increasing $C_c$. [L1, F1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: A level-$\ell$ fine path has $T/h_\ell=2^\ell$ steps and its coarse companion has $2^{\ell-1}$ steps. Each commutative Milstein step uses a fixed finite number of coefficient/derivative evaluations and Gaussian vector samples for fixed $d,m$; [L1] requires no Lévy-area sampler. Thus one correction sample has work at most $C(2^\ell+2^{\ell-1})\le C_ch_\ell^{-1}$, including the finitely many coarse initial levels after increasing $C_c$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The fine and coarse approximations in $\Delta_\ell$ use the same Brownian path and hence the same exact terminal value $X_T$. items.assessment: The example gives an explicit exponential solution and a scalar Milstein factor for arbitrary real constants. Verification includes zero initial value and zero noise coefficient, with the latter reducing the update to deterministic Euler. It makes no global strong-rate claim for these unbounded coefficients and contains no biconditional or empty-dimensional process.

claim_sections.Example:
For $\mu,\nu,x_0\in\mathbb R$, consider the geometric Brownian SDE
$$dX_t=\mu X_t\,dt+\nu X_t\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=x_0.$$
A solution is $X_t=x_0\exp((\mu-\nu^2/2)t+\nu W_t)$. On a grid step of length $h$, the scalar Milstein update is
$$Y_{n+1}=Y_n\left(1+\mu h+\nu\Delta W_n+\frac12\nu^2((\Delta W_n)^2-h)\right).$$
This example verifies the exact-solution form and the update algebra; it makes no global rate claim under the bounded-coefficient hypotheses of the strong-order theorem.

items.assessment: The example fixes the positive-time scalar sine-diffusion model at initial value pi/4 and positive grid count. Verification computes a nonzero correction, its zero mean and positive variance, and checks bounded derivatives before applying the strong-rate theorem. It is a concrete scalar example, not a biconditional or empty scheme.

claim_sections.Example:
Consider the bounded scalar multiplicative-noise SDE $dX_t=\sin(X_t)\,dW_t$ with $X_0=\pi/4$, and initialize the numerical method with $Y_0=X_0$. Fix $T>0$ and an integer $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$, and use the uniform grid $t_n=nh$ for $0\le n\le N$. At the state $Y_0=\pi/4$, its first Milstein step is
$$Y_1=\frac\pi4+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Delta W_0+\frac14((\Delta W_0)^2-h).$$
Unlike additive noise, the diffusion derivative contributes a nonzero centered correction. The hypotheses of the strong-order theorem apply to this coefficient field.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Here $b(x)=0$, $\sigma(x)=\sin x$, and $\sigma'(x)=\cos x$. At $Y_0=\pi/4$, both $\sigma(Y_0)$ and $\sigma'(Y_0)$ equal $1/\sqrt2$, so [F1] gives the stated update with correction coefficient $\frac12(1/\sqrt2)^2=1/4$. The function $\sin x$ and its derivatives through order three are bounded and continuous, so it meets the regularity premise of [L1]. [F1, L1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Here $b(x)=0$, $\sigma(x)=\sin x$, and $\sigma'(x)=\cos x$. At $Y_0=\pi/4$, both $\sigma(Y_0)$ and $\sigma'(Y_0)$ equal $1/\sqrt2$, so [F1] gives the stated update with correction coefficient $\frac12(1/\sqrt2)^2=1/4$. The function $\sin x$ and its derivatives through order three are bounded and continuous, so it meets the regularity premise of [L1].

Hence the one-step increment variance is $h/2+h^2/8$, and the derivative correction is a separate nonzero fluctuation. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

items.assessment: The example fixes two independent Brownian coordinates and h>0. Conditional Gaussian calculations divide only by positive h and positive normal densities, with endpoint subintervals handled separately. Verification obtains positive residual h squared over four after projecting on the endpoint increments, demonstrating why the needed area is not determined by them; no iff assertion is made.

claim_sections.Example:
Let $W^1,W^2$ be independent standard Brownian coordinates and solve from $(0,0)$ the two-dimensional SDE
$$dX_t^1=dW_t^1,\qquad dX_t^2=X_t^1dW_t^2.$$
Its diffusion fields are $\sigma_1(x_1,x_2)=(1,0)$ and $\sigma_2(x_1,x_2)=(0,x_1)$. They are noncommuting: $L_1\sigma_2=(0,1)$ while $L_2\sigma_1=(0,0)$. On the first step, the exact second coordinate and its Milstein Taylor increment are $I_{12}=\int_0^hW_s^1dW_s^2$. Although $I_{12}+I_{21}=\Delta W^1\Delta W^2$, the individual area term is not determined by the two endpoint increments.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The Jacobian of $\sigma_2$ sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, so $L_1\sigma_2=(0,1)$; the Jacobian of the constant field $\sigma_1$ is zero, so $L_2\sigma_1=(0,0)$. Thus commutativity fails. Starting from $X_0=(0,0)$, the first coordinate is $W_t^1$ and the second is $\int_0^tW_s^1dW_s^2$. The general Milstein Taylor update [F2] therefore has second-coordinate increment $I_{12}$ on the first step. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: The Jacobian of $\sigma_2$ sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, so $L_1\sigma_2=(0,1)$; the Jacobian of the constant field $\sigma_1$ is zero, so $L_2\sigma_1=(0,0)$. Thus commutativity fails. Starting from $X_0=(0,0)$, the first coordinate is $W_t^1$ and the second is $\int_0^tW_s^1dW_s^2$. The general Milstein Taylor update [F2] therefore has second-coordinate increment $I_{12}$ on the first step.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [L1], the endpoints determine $I_{12}+I_{21}=UV$, where $U=\Delta W^1$ and $V=\Delta W^2$. Let $\pi_n=\{0=s_0<\cdots<s_{q_n}=h\}$ be deterministic partitions with mesh $|\pi_n|\to0$, and put $S_n=\sum_{k=0}^{q_n-1}W^1_{s_k}(W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k})$. The It\^o isometry [F3] gives $\mathbb E|S_n-I_{12}|^2=\sum_k\int_{s_k}^{s_{k+1}}(s-s_k)ds\le h|\pi_n|/2\to0$. [F3, L1, given]

Dividing by the marginal density $p_h(u)$ and completing the square gives $\mathbb E[A\mid U=u]=(s/h)u$. At $s=0$ and $s=h$ the same formula follows from $A=0$ and $A=U$, respectively. For $\ell_k=s_{k+1}-s_k$, the pair $B_k=W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k}$ and $V-B_k$ has density $p_{\ell_k}(b)p_{h-\ell_k}(v-b)$ when $\ell_k<h$; completing the square gives $\mathbb E[B_k\mid V=v]=(\ell_k/h)v$, and if $\ell_k=h$ then $B_k=V$ gives the same result. Independence of the two Brownian coordinate processes [F1] makes the joint density of $(A,U,B_k,V)$ the product of these two pair densities. Dividing by $p_h(u)p_h(v)$ shows that the conditional density of $(A,B_k)$ given $(U,V)=(u,v)$ factors, so $\mathbb E[AB_k\mid U,V]=(s/h)U(\ell_k/h)V$. By [F7], step 1.2 implies $S_n\to I_{12}$ in $L^1$; conditional expectation is $L^1$-contractive by [F6], so [F5] gives $\mathbb E[I_{12}\mid\sigma(U,V)]=UV/2$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

Dividing by the marginal density $p_h(u)$ and completing the square gives $\mathbb E[A\mid U=u]=(s/h)u$. At $s=0$ and $s=h$ the same formula follows from $A=0$ and $A=U$, respectively. Thus the endpoint increments do not determine the required area sample, and any approximation has a separate error and cost. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, A1, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The Definition requires positive state dimension but explicitly permits zero equality and inequality dimensions via unique empty maps. Empty active sets make the strict-direction condition vacuous and zero-row rank vacuous. The stated tangent, linearized and critical cones and KKT equations are definitions, with no optimizer existence or arbitrary witness-family selection asserted.

claim_sections.Definition:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
claim_sections.Remarks:
This page uses $g_i\le0$ and nonnegative inequality multipliers throughout.
The equality-only Lagrange multiplier rule does not supply any inequality
multiplier assertion.

items.assessment: The Definition allows m=p=0, with full row rank vacuous at zero rows and empty inequality intersections removing those domain restrictions. Empty multiplier vectors contribute zero to the Lagrangian; properness still requires the objective finite somewhere. Relative-interior Slater and primal/dual values are definitions, not existence of an optimizer or equivalence between all qualifications.

claim_sections.Definition:
A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is trivial if $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D$;
trivial inequalities may be removed without changing the feasible set.
Unless stated otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining,
nontrivial ones. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

items.assessment: The residual Definition explicitly gives zero-dimensional vector norm zero and uses coordinate positive parts and complementarity products. The normal cone is defined only at x in the convex set, so that comparison set is nonempty. These are deterministic formulas; a vanishing residual's equivalence with KKT is proved separately rather than assumed here.

claim_sections.Definition:
Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.

items.assessment: The Statement requires R>=1 but permits every rate zero. The proof treats that empty active-clock set before taking any minimum or dividing by total rate; otherwise the positive total guarantees at least one active clock, and finite pair ties are null. Choice assumptions are the declared exponential-law ones, not selection of a minimum from an empty set.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $R\ge1$, let $r_1,\ldots,r_R\ge0$, and set $r_0=\sum_{j=1}^R r_j$. On a common probability space let $E_1,\ldots,E_R$ be independent random variables, each with the unit exponential law $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, whose survival at $t\ge0$ is $e^{-t}$. If $r_0>0$, define
$$T_*:=\min_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j},\qquad J_*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{j:r_j>0}\frac{E_j}{r_j}.$$
Then ties have probability zero, $T_*\sim\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$, $J_*$ is independent of $T_*$, and
$$\mathbb P(J_*=j)=\frac{r_j}{r_0}.$$
If $r_0=0$, every $r_j=0$ and no finite reaction clock is active.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $r_0=0$, nonnegativity of the finite sum implies every $r_j=0$, so the set of active clocks is empty and no finite candidate time is defined. [given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: If $r_0=0$, nonnegativity of the finite sum implies every $r_j=0$, so the set of active clocks is empty and no finite candidate time is defined.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Suppose $r_0>0$. For $t\ge0$, independence in [F2] and the unit exponential survival in [F1] give $\mathbb P(T_*>t)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}\mathbb P(E_j>r_jt)=\prod_{j:r_j>0}e^{-r_jt}=e^{-r_0t}.$ Thus $T_*$ has the unique law $\operatorname{Exp}(r_0)$ specified in [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For a channel $j$ with $r_j>0$, the scaled clock $E_j/r_j$ has density $r_j e^{-r_jt}$ on $t>0$ by change of variables in [F1]. Independence [F2] therefore gives the joint density that channel $j$ rings first at time $t$ as $r_j e^{-r_jt}\prod_{k\ne j:r_k>0}e^{-r_kt}=r_j e^{-r_0t}.$ Integrating over $t>0$ yields $\mathbb P(J_*=j)=r_j/r_0$, and this joint density factors as $r_0e^{-r_0t}(r_j/r_0)$, proving independence of $T_*$ and $J_*$. items.assessment: The initial state forces the countable state set nonempty. Each active-channel generator sum may nevertheless be empty at an absorbing state, where the defined process stays constant. The proof stops on finite sublevels containing the initial state and bounds event counts; independent streams use Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, without full AC or an iff claim.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be countable and let a finite-channel system be as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. For an initial state $x_0\in E$, construct its minimal reaction process recursively: at state $x$, wait an exponential time with parameter $\lambda(x)$, choose channel $j$ with probability $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$, and move to $x+\nu_j$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, remain at $x$ forever. Use an independent stream of these exponential and uniform random inputs, whose countable product law exists by Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For $V:E\to[1,\infty)$, call $V$ **proper** when $\{x:V(x)\le n\}$ is finite for every integer $n\ge1$. For this possibly unbounded $V$, define the finite local expression
$$(QV)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(V(x+\nu_j)-V(x)\bigr);$$
this does not assert that $V$ belongs to the bounded-function domain of the generator in [F1]. Suppose $QV\le cV$ for a constant $c\ge0$. Define $T_m$ as the time of the $m$th reaction event, with $T_m=\infty$ if fewer than $m$ events occur. Then the explosion time $\tau_\infty:=\lim_{m\to\infty}T_m$ satisfies $\mathbb P_{x_0}(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. No full Axiom of Choice is used.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Stop the process at $\tau_n:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\notin K_n\}$. The stopped path takes values in the finite set $F_n$ and is frozen after exit. Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. Conditional on the reaction history through time $s$, partition on the finite vector of last-used stream indices; on each part [F3] gives independence of all unused coordinates. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. The probability of at least two events within $h$ is at most $(M_nh)^2/2$ by integrating the summed first-two-event density, bounded by $M_n^2$, over the ordered two-time simplex. Since $V\le C_n$ on $F_n$, the first-event term differs from $h(QV)(x)$ by at most $C_nM_n^2h^2/2$, using $|1-e^{-z}|\le z$ for $z\ge0$; the multiple-event remainder is bounded by $2C_n(M_nh)^2/2$. Thus, uniformly over $x\in K_n$, $\mathbb E[V(X_{(s+h)\wedge\tau_n})-V(X_{s\wedge\tau_n})\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\,1_{\{s<\tau_n\}}(QV)(X_s)+O(h^2).$ Summing this identity on a uniform partition of $[0,t]$ and letting the mesh tend to zero gives $\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]=V(x_0)+\mathbb E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}(QV)(X_s)\,ds.$ The error sum is $O(th)$; the Riemann sums converge because the stopped path has finitely many jumps by step 1.1 and $QV$ is bounded on $K_n$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Set $g_n(t)=\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]$. From step 2.1, $QV\le cV$, and $V\ge1$, we obtain $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)+c\int_0^t g_n(s)\,ds.$ Here $g_n$ is bounded on each finite interval because $X_{t\wedge\tau_n}\in F_n$. Iterating the integral inequality $m$ times bounds it by $V(x_0)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(ct)^k/k!+C_n(ct)^m/m!$; the last term tends to zero and the sum tends to $V(x_0)e^{ct}$. Hence $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)e^{ct}$. [F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Set $g_n(t)=\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]$. From step 2.1, $QV\le cV$, and $V\ge1$, we obtain $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)+c\int_0^t g_n(s)\,ds.$ Here $g_n$ is bounded on each finite interval because $X_{t\wedge\tau_n}\in F_n$. Iterating the integral inequality $m$ times bounds it by $V(x_0)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(ct)^k/k!+C_n(ct)^m/m!$; the last term tends to zero and the sum tends to $V(x_0)e^{ct}$. Hence $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)e^{ct}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$ the exit state satisfies $V(X_{\tau_n})>n$, so $n\,\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le g_n(T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}$. [F4, step 3.1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$ the exit state satisfies $V(X_{\tau_n})>n$, so $n\,\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le g_n(T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix any finite $T>0$. If $\tau_\infty\le T$ but $\tau_n>T$ for some integer $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$, infinitely many events occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$, an event of probability zero by step 1.1. A countable union over such $n$ is still null, so outside it explosion by $T$ forces $\tau_n\le T$ for every sufficiently large integer $n$. Step 4.1 gives $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty\le T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}/n$ for arbitrarily large $n$, hence this probability is zero. Taking integer $T\ge1$ proves $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. The argument uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice only as declared in [A1] and [A2]; it uses no Axiom of Choice. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

If $\tau_\infty\le T$ but $\tau_n>T$ for some integer $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$, infinitely many events occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$, an event of probability zero by step 1.1. items.assessment: The theorem requires an actual initial time/state and a certified finite envelope. The proof treats zero envelope as the constant path and otherwise uses a positive-rate marked Poisson construction; zero channel rates give empty accepted regions. Product-measurable mark sets and declared stream choice principles remain explicit, with no guarantee outside the envelope.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be finite or countable, with finitely many time-dependent propensities $a_j(t,x)$ on $[0,T]$ as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Suppose a certified constant envelope $0\le\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)\le\Lambda<\infty$ holds for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in E$. Then the dominating-thinning algorithm in [[alg-dominating-thinning-for-time-varying-reaction-rates]], with an unlimited candidate budget, has the following exact conditional law from time $t$ and state $x$:

$$\mathbb P(\text{no accepted reaction in }(t,t+u]\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds\right),\qquad 0\le u\le T-t,$$

and for every Borel $B\subseteq(t,T]$ and channel $j$,

$$\mathbb P(\text{first accepted reaction time lies in }B,\ J=j\mid X_t=x,\mathcal F_t)=\int_B a_j(s,x)\exp\!\left(-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv\right)ds.$$

After a reaction, the same rule restarts at its new time and state. Candidate events on $[0,T]$ have a Poisson count of mean $\Lambda T$; accepted reactions are a subset, so there are finitely many accepted reactions almost surely and $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$. The conclusion is conditional on the stated envelope; no law is asserted when it fails.

When $\Lambda>0$, the same two conditional-law conclusions hold if, at each fixed $(s,x)$, channel $j$ is accepted on a Borel mark set $D_j(s,x)\subseteq[0,1]$, provided these sets are pairwise disjoint, have Lebesgue measure $a_j(s,x)/\Lambda$, and for each fixed state $x$ the region
$$\{(s,u)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]:u\in D_j(s,x)\}$$
is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$. The standard cumulative intervals in the algorithm are one such choice: their endpoints are finite sums of the Borel time sections $a_k(\cdot,x)/\Lambda$, so their time-mark regions are product-measurable. If $\Lambda=0$, the step 5.1 constant-path case applies. This equivalent mark-set form is used by the minimum-intensity coupling construction.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: First assume $\Lambda>0$. If the candidate interarrival increments are $E_n/\Lambda$, then for exactly $m$ candidates at ordered times $0<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le T$, the product of the $m$ exponential gap densities and the final no-candidate survival factor is $\prod_{i=1}^m\Lambda e^{-\Lambda(s_i-s_{i-1})}\cdot e^{-\Lambda(T-s_m)}=e^{-\Lambda T}\Lambda^m,$ where $s_0=0$. This is the ordered-event density in [F4]. The independent uniform marks give the conditional product-uniform mark law, so [F5] identifies the finite marked candidate pattern with a Poisson point process of intensity $\Lambda\,ds\,du$ on $(0,T]\times[0,1]$. In particular $N^*(T)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\Lambda T)$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: First assume $\Lambda>0$. If the candidate interarrival increments are $E_n/\Lambda$, then for exactly $m$ candidates at ordered times $0<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le T$, the product of the $m$ exponential gap densities and the final no-candidate survival factor is $\prod_{i=1}^m\Lambda e^{-\Lambda(s_i-s_{i-1})}\cdot e^{-\Lambda(T-s_m)}=e^{-\Lambda T}\Lambda^m,$ where $s_0=0$. This is the ordered-event density in [F4]. The independent uniform marks give the conditional product-uniform mark law, so [F5] identifies the finite marked candidate pattern with a Poisson point process of intensity $\Lambda\,ds\,du$ on $(0,T]\times[0,1]$. In particular $N^*(T)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\Lambda T)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix a state $x$ and a time $t$ before the next accepted event. For $s\in(t,t+u]$ put $b(s)=\Lambda-\lambda(s,x)\ge0$. Conditional on $m$ ordered candidate times, the probability all marks are rejected is the product of their rejection fractions. Using the ordered candidate density from step 1.1 and Tonelli [F6], the probability of no accepted candidate is $e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\int_{t<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le t+u}\prod_{i=1}^m b(s_i)\,ds_1\cdots ds_m =e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{(\int_t^{t+u}b(s)\,ds)^m}{m!} =e^{-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds}.$ The middle identity holds because the symmetric product integrand has equal integrals on the $m!$ orderings of the cube; ties form a Lebesgue-null set. This proves the displayed survival law. [F4, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

Conditional on $m$ ordered candidate times, the probability all marks are rejected is the product of their rejection fractions. Using the ordered candidate density from step 1.1 and Tonelli [F6], the probability of no accepted candidate is $e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\int_{t<s_1<\cdots<s_m\le t+u}\prod_{i=1}^m b(s_i)\,ds_1\cdots ds_m =e^{-\Lambda u}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{(\int_t^{t+u}b(s)\,ds)^m}{m!} =e^{-\int_t^{t+u}\lambda(s,x)\,ds}.$ The middle identity holds because the symmetric product integrand has equal integrals on the $m!$ orderings of the cube; ties form a Lebesgue-null set. This proves the displayed survival law.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix a channel $j$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq(t,T]$. Future candidate points after time $t$ are independent of the history through $t$; by translation of the ordered-time density in [F4], exactly $m$ candidates on $(t,T]$ have ordered-time density $e^{-\Lambda(T-t)}\Lambda^m$. For the first accepted candidate to occur at time $s\in B$ with mark in $D_j(s,x)$, all earlier candidates must be rejected, its mark must lie in a set of measure $a_j(s,x)/\Lambda$, and later candidates are unrestricted. For $k$ earlier rejected candidates, integration over their ordered times contributes $(\int_t^s b(v)\,dv)^k/k!$; for $\ell$ later unrestricted candidates, integration contributes $(\Lambda(T-s))^\ell/\ell!$. Summing the nonnegative series and using [F6], the first-event measure on $B$ is $e^{-\Lambda(T-t)}\int_B a_j(s,x)\left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(\int_t^s b(v)\,dv)^k}{k!}\right)\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\frac{(\Lambda(T-s))^\ell}{\ell!}\right)ds =\int_B a_j(s,x)e^{-\int_t^s\lambda(v,x)\,dv}\,ds.$ This proves the channel-specific first-event law for arbitrary Borel rates and for disjoint mark sets of the specified measures whose time-mark regions are product-measurable; their locations within $[0,1]$ do not enter the calculation. The endpoint mark conventions differ only on a null set. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At an accepted candidate time the new state depends only on the past and that candidate's mark. If its candidate index is $K$, the event $\{K=n\}$ is determined by the first $n$ gap and mark coordinates; partitioning over finite $n$ shows that the coordinates after $K$ retain their prescribed product law. Thus the same two calculations restart at the new state and time. Since $N(T)\le N^*(T)$ pathwise, [F7] gives $\mathbb E N(T)\le\Lambda T$ and $N(T)<\infty$ almost surely. items.assessment: The algorithms start from an admitted state, excluding an empty state-space instance. Their active-channel generator sums can be empty when total rate is zero, and the proof returns the absorbing path before a rate division. Marked zero-increment events remain counted. The conclusion is equality of path laws under supplied streams, not an iff or an arbitrary process choice.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and let $E$ be finite with a reaction system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. Supply the independent random streams required by [[alg-gillespie-direct-method-for-reaction-networks]] and [[alg-next-reaction-random-time-change-method]]. Define the reference marked process recursively: at state $x$, if $\lambda(x)>0$, its next reaction time has law $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda(x))$ and its channel is independent of that time with probabilities $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, it remains at $x$. Then both algorithms have the law of this reference process on every finite horizon. The process has generator operator
$$(Qf)(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr),$$
absorbing states are handled exactly, and for $\Lambda=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$ the expected total reaction count on $[0,T]$ is at most $\Lambda T$. A zero-increment channel is still a marked reaction event, but it contributes zero to the state generator.

items.assessment: The Statement supplies both initial states and finite systems, so neither coordinate state set is empty. The proof returns two constant paths if the candidate envelope is zero; otherwise nested fixed mark intervals give the exact shared/residual rates and marginal laws. It constructs a particular coupling from declared streams, not a choice from an unspecified coupling family.

claim_sections.Statement: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite-state reaction systems with the same $R$ channel labels, respective increments $\nu_j^X,\nu_j^Y$ and propensities $a_j^X(x),a_j^Y(y)$, and fixed initial states $(x_0,y_0)$. Run [[alg-minimum-intensity-coupling-for-reaction-networks]] with an unlimited candidate budget. Then each coordinate path has exactly the law of its own reaction process run by the Gillespie direct method. At each pair state $(x,y)$ and channel $j$, shared events have rate $\min(a_j^X(x),a_j^Y(y))$, $X$-only events have rate $(a_j^X(x)-a_j^Y(y))_+$, and $Y$-only events have rate $(a_j^Y(y)-a_j^X(x))_+$. The expected total number of paired candidates on $[0,T]$ is $MT$, where $M=\sum_jM_j$ is defined in the algorithm; hence the coupled construction has finitely many events almost surely. If $M=0$, both paths are constant.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $M=0$, every $M_j=0$, so all propensities in both systems vanish and the constant paths are exact. Suppose $M>0$. The candidate process has rate $M$. For channel $j$, its mark block has length $M_j/M$, and the $X$-acceptance portion has length $(M_j/M)(a_j^X(x)/M_j)=a_j^X(x)/M$; the corresponding $Y$ portion has length $a_j^Y(y)/M$. These are disjoint across channels for either coordinate and depend only on that coordinate's own current state. [A1, A2, F2, given, algebra]

items.assessment: The state set is explicitly finite nonempty, but individual active rates and all counts may vanish. The proof treats zero global envelope first, builds predictable compensators from bounded state rates, and extends finite simple-integrand identities through declared AC interfaces. The finite channel sum includes zero integrands; this is an isometry and bracket theorem, not a biconditional.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice for the conditional-expectation, martingale and stochastic-integral interfaces, and Countable Choice and Dependent Choice for the independent input streams. Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state set, let a finite-channel reaction system be as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], and set $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)$. Let $X$ be the process generated by the unlimited-budget Gillespie method, using its equivalent dominating-thinning realization with candidate rate $\Lambda$ and the natural filtration of candidate times and marks. For each channel $j$, define
$$N_j(t):=\#\{s\le t:\text{a channel-}j\text{ reaction occurs at }s\},\quad A_j(t):=\int_0^t a_j(X_{s-})\,ds,\quad M_j(t):=N_j(t)-A_j(t).$$
Then each $N_j$ is a simple counting process, $A_j$ is a continuous predictable compensator with $\mathbb E A_j(T)<\infty$, and $M_j$ is a square-integrable martingale. Its optional bracket and continuous predictable bracket are $[M_j]_t=N_j(t)$ and $\langle M_j\rangle_t=A_j(t)$. For distinct channels $i\ne j$, $[M_i,M_j]_t=\langle M_i,M_j\rangle_t=0$.

For any finite family of predictable real processes $H_1,\ldots,H_R$ satisfying
$$\sum_{j=1}^R\mathbb E\int_0^T H_j(s)^2a_j(X_{s-})\,ds<\infty,$$
the $L^2$ integrals against each $M_j$ exist and satisfy
$$\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^R\int_0^T H_j(s)\,dM_j(s)\right)^2\right]=\sum_{j=1}^R\mathbb E\int_0^T H_j(s)^2a_j(X_{s-})\,ds.$$
Zero-increment channels remain counted as marked events and obey these same formulas.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $\mathcal G_t$ be generated by candidate times and marks up to $t$; these sigma-algebras increase with $t$, so [F5] makes them a continuous-time filtration. If $\Lambda=0$, all rates and all counts vanish. Otherwise the thinning realization has a rate-$\Lambda$ candidate process, and [F2] gives the same reaction path law as Gillespie. By [F3], candidates have no ties and their number on $[0,T]$ is finite almost surely. Hence each $N_j$ is adapted, nondecreasing and integer-valued with unit jumps and finite terminal value; also $N_j(T)\le N^*(T)$ and $0\le A_j(T)\le\Lambda T$. The state path is piecewise constant with finitely many jumps. Its left-limit process $X_{s-}$ is a pointwise limit of left-grid processes taking the value $X_{k2^{-n}}$ on $(k2^{-n},(k+1)2^{-n}]$; each is measurable for the generators in [F4]. Thus $a_j(X_{s-})$ is predictable. Because the density is bounded and piecewise constant along the path, for fixed $t$ its time integral is the limit of left-grid Riemann sums of values known by time $t$, so $A_j(t)$ is $\mathcal G_t$-measurable. The integral is continuous and bounded by $\Lambda T$; continuous adapted processes are pointwise limits of their left-grid predictable approximations, so $A_j$ is predictable with finite mean. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix deterministic $s$ and $0<h\le T-s$, and condition on $\mathcal G_s$ with $X_s=x$. The first accepted channel-$j$ event has density $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$ at elapsed time $u$, by [F2]. Its probability over $0<u\le h$ differs from $a_j(x)h$ by at most $a_j(x)\lambda(x)h^2/2\le\Lambda^2h^2/2$. Further channel-$j$ events require at least two candidates; if $N^*$ is their count and $\mu=\Lambda h$, then [F3] gives $\mathbb E(N^*1_{\{N^*\ge2\}})=\mu(1-e^{-\mu})\le\mu^2$. Therefore $\left|\mathbb E(N_j(s+h)-N_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)-a_j(x)h\right|\le\tfrac32\Lambda^2h^2.$ If no candidate occurs in $(s,s+h]$, the state stays at $x$ and the compensator increment equals $a_j(x)h$. Otherwise both that increment and $a_j(x)h$ lie between $0$ and $\Lambda h$, while the conditional probability of a candidate is at most $\Lambda h$. Therefore $\left|\mathbb E(A_j(s+h)-A_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)-a_j(x)h\right|\le\Lambda^2h^2,$ so $|\mathbb E(M_j(s+h)-M_j(s)\mid\mathcal G_s)|\le\tfrac52\Lambda^2h^2$. For $B\in\mathcal G_s$, partition $[s,t]$ into intervals of mesh at most $\delta$; conditional expectation on each left endpoint bounds $|\mathbb E(1_B(M_j(t)-M_j(s)))|$ by $\tfrac52\Lambda^2\delta(t-s)$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives zero for every $B\in\mathcal G_s$, which is the all-pairs martingale identity. Since $N_j(T)\le N^*(T)$ and $A_j(T)\le\Lambda T$, the bound $M_j(T)^2\le2N_j(T)^2+2A_j(T)^2$ and [F3] give $\mathbb E M_j(T)^2<\infty$; the same bound applies at every $t\le T$. Thus $M_j$ is square-integrable. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

Steps 1.1–2.1 verify the simple-count, finite-mean continuous predictable compensator, and square-integrable martingale hypotheses of [F6]. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For bounded predictable step integrands $H_i,H_j$ on a common deterministic partition, expand $\mathbb E(I_iI_j)$, where $I_i=\int H_i\,dM_i$. Terms from distinct time intervals vanish by conditioning on the left endpoint of the later interval and using the martingale property from step 2.1. On an interval of length $h$, the same-interval product has conditional absolute expectation at most $5\Lambda^2h^2$: the product of distinct channel counts is zero unless at least two candidates occur, whose $N^{*2}$ expectation is $\mu^2+\mu(1-e^{-\mu})\le2\mu^2$; the two count-compensator terms are each at most $\Lambda h\,\mathbb E(N^*\mid\mathcal G_s)\le\Lambda^2h^2$, and the compensator product is at most $\Lambda^2h^2$. If the step coefficients are bounded in absolute value by $K$, multiplying by them gives a bound $5K^2\Lambda^2h^2$. Refining the common partition leaves each step integral unchanged and makes the sum of these bounds tend to zero, so $\mathbb E(I_iI_j)=0$. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For general $H_j$ in the stated finite-energy class, [F10] supplies bounded predictable step approximations in each compensator $L^2$ norm. By [F9], their individual integrals converge in $L^2$ to $I_j=\int_0^T H_j\,dM_j$ and satisfy $\mathbb E I_j^2=\mathbb E\int_0^T H_j^2\,dA_j$. items.assessment: The counterexample fixes the infinite nonempty positive-integer state set and one active channel with rate n squared. Holding-time sums begin at n=1, so no zero holding-time denominator occurs; explicit exponential expectations and monotone convergence give finite explosion time. The example uses the stated stream choice principles and refutes sufficiency of finite per-state rates only.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $E=\{1,2,\ldots\}$, use one increment $\nu=1$, and set the propensity $a(n)=n^2$. Starting at $X_0=1$, the minimal reaction process has explosion time
$$\tau_\infty=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}W_n,$$
where the independent holding times satisfy $W_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(n^2)$. This sum is finite almost surely, so finite per-state rates alone do not prevent explosion. The sufficient criterion in [[thm-countable-state-reaction-networks-lyapunov-nonexplosion]] does not apply with $V(n)=n$, since its local expression $QV(n)=n^2$ is not bounded by $cn$ for any finite $c$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At state $n$, the only active channel has finite rate $n^2$ and moves to $n+1\in E$, so [F1] defines a valid countable-state network. With independent unit exponentials $E_n$, its $n$th holding time is $W_n=E_n/n^2$; [F2] gives the stated law and the recursive path visits $1,2,3,\ldots$ until its limiting time. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, construct]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The density of $W_n$ is $n^2e^{-n^2t}$ for $t>0$. For $b>0$, [F5] and differentiation of the displayed antiderivative give $\mathbb E[W_n\mathbf1_{\{W_n\le b\}}]=\int_0^b t n^2e^{-n^2t}\,dt=\frac{1-(n^2b+1)e^{-n^2b}}{n^2}.$ As $b\to\infty$, $(n^2b+1)e^{-n^2b}\to0$: setting $u=n^2b$, the exponential series gives $e^u\ge u^3/6$, so $(u+1)e^{-u}\le6(u+1)/u^3\to0$. Applying [F4] to the increasing truncations yields $\mathbb E W_n=1/n^2$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

Applying [F4] to the increasing truncations yields $\mathbb E W_n=1/n^2$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $n\ge2$, $1/n^2\le1/(n(n-1))=1/(n-1)-1/n$. Therefore $\mathbb E\sum_{n=1}^mW_n=\sum_{n=1}^m1/n^2\le2$. Since the partial sums increase, [F4] gives $\mathbb E\tau_\infty=\mathbb E\lim_m\sum_{n=1}^mW_n\le2$. If $p=\mathbb P(\tau_\infty=\infty)>0$, then $\mathbb E\tau_\infty\ge kp$ for every integer $k$, contradicting this finite bound. Thus $\tau_\infty<\infty$ almost surely. [F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

items.assessment: The fixed one-state example has one zero-increment marked channel at positive rate two and an invalid envelope one. Its proof compares distinct exponential survivals for t>0 and preserves the algorithm's invalid-envelope status instead of clipping. Singleton state/channel sizes are built into the example, not an iff or arbitrary-selection assertion.

claim_sections.Statement: Consider the one-state system $E=\{0\}$ with one zero-increment channel $\nu=0$ and constant propensity $a(t,0)=2$. Its first marked reaction time has survival $e^{-2t}$. If an implementation incorrectly uses the understated envelope $\Lambda=1$ and clips the acceptance probability $a/\Lambda=2$ to $1$, it accepts every rate-one candidate, so its first marked reaction time has survival $e^{-t}$. These laws differ for every $t>0$. The specified algorithm requires a valid envelope and does not clip: a detected violation returns `invalid-envelope`, and the exact-thinning theorem asserts no law under a failed envelope.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The target system has constant total rate $2$; [F4] therefore gives its first marked-event survival $e^{-2t}$. This is an event even though $\nu=0$, by [F1]. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: A rate-one candidate process has no candidate by time $t$ with probability $e^{-t}$. The clipped rule accepts every candidate, hence its first accepted-event survival is $e^{-t}$; for $t>0$, $e^{-t}\ne e^{-2t}$. Thus clipping changes the event law. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

items.assessment: The fixed two-state one-channel death process moves from one to zero after a unit exponential wait. Verification handles zero propensity by the absorbing-path status and computes its two probabilities at every t>=0. No division by zero rate, endpoint convention beyond this stated time range, or arbitrary state/process choice is used.

claim_sections.Statement: Let $E=\{0,1\}$ with one death channel of increment $-1$, propensity $a(1)=1$, and $a(0)=0$. Starting from $1$, the process waits an $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ time $W$, moves to $0$, and remains there forever. In particular, state $0$ has total hazard zero and is absorbing.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The only positive rate is $a(1)=1$, and its poststate $1+(-1)=0$ lies in $E$, so the system is admissible. At $1$, [F2] gives $W\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$; at $0$, the total rate is $0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Once the first event occurs, the state is $0$ and every propensity is zero. items.assessment: The fixed three-state birth/death model has total rate two everywhere. Verification checks zero birth rate at the upper state and zero death rate at the lower state before evaluating poststates, and computes the first-event threshold and generator. The specified finite input and exact streams introduce no iff or arbitrary witness selection.

claim_sections.Statement: Let $E=\{0,1,2\}$ with a birth channel $\nu_+=1$, $a_+(x)=2-x$, and a death channel $\nu_-=-1$, $a_-(x)=x$. From every state the total rate is $2$. Starting at $1$, the first holding time is $E_1/2$; the event is a birth if $U_1<1/2$ and a death otherwise. The direct method generates the exact finite-state reaction path law.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $x<2$, the birth rate $2-x$ is positive and $x+1\in E$; at $x=2$ its rate is zero. For $x>0$, the death rate $x$ is positive and $x-1\in E$; at $x=0$ its rate is zero. Thus both channels are admissible, and $a_+(x)+a_-(x)=2$ for all $x\in E$. [F1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For $x<2$, the birth rate $2-x$ is positive and $x+1\in E$; at $x=2$ its rate is zero. For $x>0$, the death rate $x$ is positive and $x-1\in E$; at $x=0$ its rate is zero. Thus both channels are admissible, and $a_+(x)+a_-(x)=2$ for all $x\in E$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At state $1$ the two propensities are each $1$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

items.assessment: The fixed pair of three-state systems starts at (1,1). Verification checks boundary-disabled channels, three unit-rate accepted events and a candidate envelope six, with one residual event type having rate zero. The explicit mark construction gives first-event rate three and exact marginals; it is not an iff or arbitrary coupling choice.

claim_sections.Statement:
On $E_X=E_Y=\{0,1,2\}$, let both chains have birth increment $+1$ and death increment $-1$. Set
$$a_+^X(x)=2-x,\quad a_-^X(x)=x,\qquad a_+^Y(y)=2-y,\quad a_-^Y(y)=2y.$$
Starting from $(1,1)$, the minimum-intensity coupling has at the first paired event three possibilities, each at rate $1$: shared birth to $(2,2)$, shared death to $(0,0)$, or $Y$-only death to $(1,0)$. Thus its first paired-event time is $\operatorname{Exp}(3)$ and each possibility has probability $1/3$. The coordinate path marginals remain the exact $X$ and $Y$ reaction laws.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For both systems, a positive birth rate occurs only at $x<2$ and moves to $x+1\in E$; a positive death rate occurs only at $x>0$ and moves to $x-1\in E$. All rates are nonnegative and finite, so [F1] gives valid finite-state systems. [F1, given, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For both systems, a positive birth rate occurs only at $x<2$ and moves to $x+1\in E$; a positive death rate occurs only at $x>0$ and moves to $x-1\in E$. All rates are nonnegative and finite, so [F1] gives valid finite-state systems.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At $(1,1)$ the birth rates are $1,1$, hence [F2] gives shared birth rate $1$. items.assessment: The Statement has a real center and positive step with both symmetric stencil points in the open domain. The proof cancels even Taylor terms and divides only by positive 2h, retaining zero derivative/remainder constants. It constructs a remainder from two fixed evaluations, not arbitrary witness families or an iff.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, let $x\in I$, and let $h>0$ with $[x-h,x+h]\subset I$. Suppose $f\in C^5$ on a neighborhood of this interval and $|f^{(5)}(y)|\le M_5$ throughout it. Then for some real $r_h$,

$$D_h^0f(x)=f'(x)+c_2h^2+r_h,\qquad c_2:=\frac{f'''(x)}6,\qquad |r_h|\le \frac{M_5h^4}{120}.$$

The same coefficient $c_2$ works for every admissible $h$ at the fixed point $x$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F2] at $x$ to $x+h$ and $x-h$. The degree-four Taylor polynomials subtract to $2hf'(x)+h^3f'''(x)/3$, because the constant, quadratic and fourth-degree terms agree at the two endpoints. Each remainder has magnitude at most $M_5h^5/120$. [given, F2, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Apply [F2] at $x$ to $x+h$ and $x-h$. The degree-four Taylor polynomials subtract to $2hf'(x)+h^3f'''(x)/3$, because the constant, quadratic and fourth-degree terms agree at the two endpoints. Each remainder has magnitude at most $M_5h^5/120$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [F3]–[F4], the difference of the two remainders has magnitude at most $2M_5h^5/120$. Divide the subtracted expansion by $2h$ and use [F1]: the remainder in $D_h^0f(x)$ is bounded by $M_5h^4/120$, and the cubic term becomes $f'''(x)h^2/6$. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [F3]–[F4], the difference of the two remainders has magnitude at most $2M_5h^5/120$. Divide the subtracted expansion by $2h$ and use [F1]: the remainder in $D_h^0f(x)$ is bounded by $M_5h^4/120$, and the cubic term becomes $f'''(x)h^2/6$.

items.assessment: The Statement requires holomorphy, real-axis reality and h>0 on a supplied vertical segment. The proof obtains zero initial imaginary value/second derivative and divides the Taylor expansion by positive h. Evaluation error is a separate allowed nonnegative term; no claim is made at zero step or without holomorphy, and no equivalence is asserted.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $x\in U\cap\mathbb R$, and suppose $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, real-valued on a real interval $I\subseteq U\cap\mathbb R$ around $x$, and $\{x+it:0\le t\le h\}\subset U$ for $h>0$. Suppose $|\operatorname{Re}f'''(x+it)|\le M_3$ for $0\le t\le h$, with $M_3\ge0$. Then

$$|C_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}.$$

If the evaluated imaginary component has error at most $\delta_{\rm im}$, then

$$|\widehat C_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}+\frac{\delta_{\rm im}}h.$$

Holomorphy and real-axis reality are essential to the formula: real differentiability of the restriction alone is insufficient.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Put $g(t):=\operatorname{Im}f(x+it)$ for $0\le t\le h$. By [F4], its coordinate functions are smooth. By [F3], $g'(t)=v_y(x,t)=u_x(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}f'(x+it)$. If $q=p+ir$ is holomorphic, [F3] gives $\partial_y p=-\partial_xr=-\operatorname{Im}q'$ and $\partial_y r=\partial_xp=\operatorname{Re}q'$. Applying [F5] to $f$ and then to $f'$ makes $f'$ and $f''$ holomorphic, so these identities give $g''(t)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x+it)$ and $g'''(t)=-\operatorname{Re}f'''(x+it)$. [given, F3, F4, F5, construct]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Put $g(t):=\operatorname{Im}f(x+it)$ for $0\le t\le h$. By [F4], its coordinate functions are smooth. By [F3], $g'(t)=v_y(x,t)=u_x(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}f'(x+it)$. If $q=p+ir$ is holomorphic, [F3] gives $\partial_y p=-\partial_xr=-\operatorname{Im}q'$ and $\partial_y r=\partial_xp=\operatorname{Re}q'$. Applying [F5] to $f$ and then to $f'$ makes $f'$ and $f''$ holomorphic, so these identities give $g''(t)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x+it)$ and $g'''(t)=-\operatorname{Re}f'''(x+it)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At real arguments near $x$, $f$ is real by hypothesis, so its real-direction difference quotients show that $f'$ is real there; applying the same argument to the holomorphic function $f'$ shows that $f''$ is real there. Thus $g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=f'(x)$, and $g''(0)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x)=0$. By step 1.1, $|g'''(t)|\le M_3$ on $[0,h]$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: At real arguments near $x$, $f$ is real by hypothesis, so its real-direction difference quotients show that $f'$ is real there; applying the same argument to the holomorphic function $f'$ shows that $f''$ is real there. Thus $g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=f'(x)$, and $g''(0)=-\operatorname{Im}f''(x)=0$. By step 1.1, $|g'''(t)|\le M_3$ on $[0,h]$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F6] to $g$ from $0$ to $h$. For some $\xi\in(0,h)$, $g(h)=h f'(x)+g'''(\xi)h^3/6$. Since $h>0$, [F8] gives $|g(h)/h-f'(x)|=|g'''(\xi)|h^2/6\le M_3h^2/6$. By [F1] and [F7], $g(h)/h=C_hf(x)$, proving the exact complex-step error bound. [given, F1, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Apply [F6] to $g$ from $0$ to $h$. For some $\xi\in(0,h)$, $g(h)=h f'(x)+g'''(\xi)h^3/6$. Since $h>0$, [F8] gives $|g(h)/h-f'(x)|=|g'''(\xi)|h^2/6\le M_3h^2/6$. By [F1] and [F7], $g(h)/h=C_hf(x)$, proving the exact complex-step error bound.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [F1] and [F8], $|\widehat C_hf(x)-C_hf(x)|\le\delta_{\rm im}/h$. [F9] and step 3.1 give the inexact bound. [given, F1, F8, F9, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [F1] and [F8], $|\widehat C_hf(x)-C_hf(x)|\le\delta_{\rm im}/h$. [F9] and step 3.1 give the inexact bound.

items.assessment: The Statement assumes positive step and the appropriate nonempty real stencil segment. The proof applies Taylor at fixed endpoints and bounds evaluation differences by the triangle inequality, allowing zero derivative/error bounds. It supplies sufficient inequalities, not exact-error equivalences, and no choice of independent random noise is silently made.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $x\in I$, and $h>0$. For the forward bound assume $[x,x+h]\subset I$, $f\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of that interval, and $|f''(y)|\le M_2$ there. For the central bound assume $[x-h,x+h]\subset I$, $f\in C^3$ on a neighborhood of that interval, and $|f'''(y)|\le M_3$ there. Then

$$|D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_2h}{2},\qquad |D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}.$$

If each function evaluation has absolute error at most $\delta\ge0$ as in [[def-finite-difference-stencils-and-evaluation-error-model]], then

$$|\widehat D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_2h}{2}+\frac{2\delta}{h},\qquad |\widehat D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{M_3h^2}{6}+\frac{2\delta}{h}.$$

For the central stencil the evaluation contribution is in fact at most $\delta/h$; the displayed $2\delta/h$ is a uniform conservative bound for both stencils.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F2] with $n=1$, $a=x$, and $y=x+h$. Then $f(x+h)=f(x)+hf'(x)+h^2f''(\xi)/2$ for some $\xi\in(x,x+h)$. Substituting into [F1] gives $D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)=hf''(\xi)/2$, so the forward truncation bound follows. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Apply [F2] with $n=1$, $a=x$, and $y=x+h$. Then $f(x+h)=f(x)+hf'(x)+h^2f''(\xi)/2$ for some $\xi\in(x,x+h)$. Substituting into [F1] gives $D_h^+f(x)-f'(x)=hf''(\xi)/2$, so the forward truncation bound follows.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply [F2] with $n=2$ to $y=x+h$ and $y=x-h$. Subtracting the two expansions cancels the equal even-order terms and gives $D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)=h^2(f'''(\xi_+)+f'''(\xi_-))/12$ for intermediate points $\xi_+\in(x,x+h)$ and $\xi_-\in(x-h,x)$. The derivative bound and [F3]–[F4] give magnitude at most $M_3h^2/6$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Apply [F2] with $n=2$ to $y=x+h$ and $y=x-h$. Subtracting the two expansions cancels the equal even-order terms and gives $D_h^0f(x)-f'(x)=h^2(f'''(\xi_+)+f'''(\xi_-))/12$ for intermediate points $\xi_+\in(x,x+h)$ and $\xi_-\in(x-h,x)$. The derivative bound and [F3]–[F4] give magnitude at most $M_3h^2/6$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Write the forward evaluation errors as $e_+=e_{x+h}$ and $e_0=e_x$. By [F1], $\widehat D_h^+-D_h^+=(e_+-e_0)/h$; [F3]–[F4] bound its magnitude by $2\delta/h$. The triangle inequality with step 1.1 proves the forward inexact bound. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Write the forward evaluation errors as $e_+=e_{x+h}$ and $e_0=e_x$. By [F1], $\widehat D_h^+-D_h^+=(e_+-e_0)/h$; [F3]–[F4] bound its magnitude by $2\delta/h$. The triangle inequality with step 1.1 proves the forward inexact bound.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Write the central errors as $e_+=e_{x+h}$ and $e_-=e_{x-h}$. Then $\widehat D_h^0-D_h^0=(e_+-e_-)/(2h)$, whose magnitude is at most $\delta/h$ by [F1], [F3] and [F4], hence at most $2\delta/h$. Combining with step 1.2 proves the stated central inexact bound. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Write the central errors as $e_+=e_{x+h}$ and $e_-=e_{x-h}$. Then $\widehat D_h^0-D_h^0=(e_+-e_-)/(2h)$, whose magnitude is at most $\delta/h$ by [F1], [F3] and [F4], hence at most $2\delta/h$. Combining with step 1.2 proves the stated central inexact bound.

items.assessment: The Statement requires positive input/output dimensions and step, but permits zero direction and zero evaluation errors. The proof combines fixed component Taylor bounds in Euclidean norm and separately derives variance from centered covariance data, reserving independence for its stated specialization. Degenerate covariance is not divided out, and no iff or arbitrary sample selection is claimed.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $m,n\ge1$, $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $x\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and $h>0$ with the required line segments contained in $U$. Use the estimators of [[def-jacobian-and-hessian-vector-difference-products]]. For a vector-valued map, $F\in C^k(U)$ means that each component $F_i$ is in $C^k(U)$. For $F\in C^2$, suppose each component $g_i(t):=F_i(x+tv)$ satisfies $|g_i''(t)|\le b_{2,i}$ for $0\le t\le h$, with $b_{2,i}\ge0$; put $M_{2,F}:=(\sum_{i<m} b_{2,i}^2)^{1/2}$. For $F\in C^3$, suppose $|g_i'''(t)|\le b_{3,i}$ for $-h\le t\le h$, with $b_{3,i}\ge0$; put $M_{3,F}:=(\sum_{i<m} b_{3,i}^2)^{1/2}$. Then

$$\|J_h^+(F,x,v)-JF(x)v\|_2\le M_{2,F}h/2,\qquad \|J_h^0(F,x,v)-JF(x)v\|_2\le M_{3,F}h^2/6.$$

For $f\in C^3$, set $q_j(t):=\partial_jf(x+tv)$, suppose $|q_j''(t)|\le a_{2,j}$ on $[0,h]$, with $a_{2,j}\ge0$, and put $M_{2,H}:=(\sum_{j<n} a_{2,j}^2)^{1/2}$. For $f\in C^4$, suppose $|q_j'''(t)|\le a_{3,j}$ on $[-h,h]$, with $a_{3,j}\ge0$, and put $M_{3,H}:=(\sum_{j<n} a_{3,j}^2)^{1/2}$. Then

$$\|H_h^+(f,x,v)-H_f(x)v\|_2\le M_{2,H}h/2,\qquad \|H_h^0(f,x,v)-H_f(x)v\|_2\le M_{3,H}h^2/6.$$

If each vector evaluation has Euclidean error at most $\delta$, the forward evaluation contribution is at most $2\delta/h$ and the central contribution at most $\delta/h$ (hence also at most $2\delta/h$). For a scalar output coordinate on a common probability space, suppose its two square-integrable evaluation noises are centered, with variances $\sigma_1^2,\sigma_0^2$ and covariance $c$. Their forward-difference noise variance is $(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_0^2-2c)/h^2$; the central formula has the same numerator divided by $4h^2$. If these centered noises are independent and both have variance $\sigma^2$, then the formulas reduce to $2\sigma^2/h^2$ forward and $\sigma^2/(2h^2)$ central. No variance sum or root-sum-square total-error claim is made without the stated centering and covariance information.

If every evaluation call used in a given estimate has Euclidean error at most a common $\delta\ge0$, then the inexact estimates of [[def-jacobian-and-hessian-vector-difference-products]] satisfy

$$\|\widehat J_h^+(F,x,v)-JF(x)v\|_2\le M_{2,F}h/2+2\delta/h,\qquad \|\widehat J_h^0(F,x,v)-JF(x)v\|_2\le M_{3,F}h^2/6+\delta/h,$$

$$\|\widehat H_h^+(f,x,v)-H_f(x)v\|_2\le M_{2,H}h/2+2\delta/h,\qquad \|\widehat H_h^0(f,x,v)-H_f(x)v\|_2\le M_{3,H}h^2/6+\delta/h.$$

The central evaluation contribution is at most $\delta/h$, so the conservative $2\delta/h$ contribution is also valid for the central estimates.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let the objects and notation be those of [[def-structural-column-coloring-for-sparse-jacobian-recovery]], and suppose $\chi$ is a proper coloring of the graph of a safe structural row pattern. For every row $0\le i<m$, every color $c$, and every column $j\in S_i$ with $\chi(j)=c$,

$$J_{ij}=(Js^c)_i.$$

Entries with $j\notin S_i$ are zero by the safe-pattern hypothesis. Thus all entries are recovered from one compressed product per color. A color collision in a row does not give a general recovery guarantee: two distinct Jacobians supported on that colliding row can have the same compressed product.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $H>0$. Consider the conservative error bounds from [[thm-forward-and-central-difference-truncation-and-evaluation-error-bounds]] on a permitted step interval $(0,H]$, where every stencil with $h\le H$ stays inside the domain. If $M_2>0$ and $\delta>0$, the forward bound

$$E_+(h)=M_2h/2+2\delta/h$$

has the unique unconstrained minimizer $h_+=\sqrt{4\delta/M_2}$ and minimum $2\sqrt{M_2\delta}$. On $(0,H]$ the minimizer is $\min\{h_+,H\}$. If $M_3>0$ and $\delta>0$, the central conservative bound

$$E_0(h)=M_3h^2/6+2\delta/h$$

has the unique unconstrained minimizer $h_0=\sqrt[3]{6\delta/M_3}$ and minimum $M_3h_0^2/2$; on $(0,H]$ the minimizer is $\min\{h_0,H\}$. These optimize the displayed error bounds, not the unknown actual error.

If $\delta=0$ and the corresponding truncation constant is positive, the bound has infimum $0$ as $h\downarrow0$ and no minimizer for $h>0$. If the corresponding truncation constant is $0$ and $\delta>0$, the bound decreases with $h$, so its capped minimum is at $H$. If $\delta$ and the corresponding truncation constant are both zero, every permitted step is optimal.

Since $r+r^{-1}-2=(r-1)^2/r\ge0$, equality holds exactly at $r=1$. Thus $h_+$ is the unique unconstrained minimizer and its value is $2\sqrt{M_2\delta}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $x\in I$, and $h>0$ with $[x-h,x+h]\subset I$. Suppose that for every $0<t\le h$ the central difference has the actual uniform expansion

$$D_t^0f(x)=f'(x)+c_2t^2+r_t,\qquad |r_t|\le Mt^4,$$

where $c_2$ and $M\ge0$ do not depend on $t$. Then the Richardson estimate of [[def-richardson-extrapolation-under-a-fourth-order-remainder]] satisfies

$$|R_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{5Mh^4}{12}.$$

In particular, under [[lem-central-difference-has-fourth-order-remainder-under-bounded-fifth-derivative]] the bound holds with $c_2=f'''(x)/6$ and $M=M_5/120$, giving $|R_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le M_5h^4/288$. If the four function values used at $x\pm h/2$ and $x\pm h$ each have absolute error at most $\delta$, then

$$|\widehat R_hf(x)-f'(x)|\le \frac{5Mh^4}{12}+\frac{3\delta}{h}.$$

items.assessment: The theorem accepts integer dimension candidates and finite arrays, returning invalid-dimension before scans if needed. Its proof counts finite pointer/index scans and disjoint stored-index ranges; on valid zero-row input no accumulation is entered. claim_sections.Statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, and let $r,c,v,x$ be finite
candidate arrays, with entries of $v$ and $x$ in $F$. The algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] terminates on every such
input. Its return status is `invalid-dimension`, `invalid-index`, or `ok` with
a vector in $F^m$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If a dimension is not natural or an array length fails its dimension check, the algorithm returns `invalid-dimension` immediately. Otherwise $m,n$ and $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$ are finite naturals by [L1]. The row-pointer and column-index validations inspect at most $m+1$ and $s$ entries, respectively, and each scan advances its index by one; therefore they finish and either return `invalid-index` or pass as in [L2]. [given, L1, L2, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: If a dimension is not natural or an array length fails its dimension check, the algorithm returns `invalid-dimension` immediately. Otherwise $m,n$ and $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$ are finite naturals by [L1]. The row-pointer and column-index validations inspect at most $m+1$ and $s$ entries, respectively, and each scan advances its index by one; therefore they finish and either return `invalid-index` or pass as in [L2].

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If validation passes, the outer loop has $m$ iterations. The inner ranges are disjoint and their total length is $\sum_{i<m}(r_{i+1}-r_i)=r_m-r_0=s$, so all accumulation loops in [L3] are finite and every accessed index is valid. The algorithm then returns `ok` with its length-$m$ output. Together with step 1.1 this proves termination on every input in the Statement. [given, L3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

The algorithm then returns `ok` with its length-$m$ output. Together with step 1.1 this proves termination on every input in the Statement.

items.assessment: The theorem works over an arbitrary field with natural row/column counts, including zero. Its proof starts each row with the empty sum, distributes/reindexes stored contributions including duplicates, and explicitly equates the unique empty outputs when m=0. There is no interval parameter, biconditional, or unprescribed witness selection in this exact-product identity.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Define
$(Ax)_i:=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j$, the usual matrix-vector product from
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix a row $i$. Initially its output coordinate is $0_F$, the empty partial sum. After $q$ entries of that row have been visited, induction on $q$ gives $y_i=\sum_{t=r_i}^{r_i+q-1}v_t x_{c_t}$: the next algorithmic update adds exactly the next summand. Taking $q=r_{i+1}-r_i$ yields $y_i=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$. [L2, induction, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Fix a row $i$. Initially its output coordinate is $0_F$, the empty partial sum. After $q$ entries of that row have been visited, induction on $q$ gives $y_i=\sum_{t=r_i}^{r_i+q-1}v_t x_{c_t}$: the next algorithmic update adds exactly the next summand. Taking $q=r_{i+1}-r_i$ yields $y_i=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [L1] and [L3], $(Ax)_i=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t x_j$. Repeated application of [L5], by induction on the finite number of summands, distributes the products over these sums. Re-enumerating the resulting finite sum over pairs $(j,t)$ as $(t,j)$ is permitted by [L4]. For each fixed $t$, exactly the term $j=c_t$ survives, so the result is $\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$. By step 1.1 this equals $y_i$. [L1, L3, L4, L5, L7, L8, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [L1] and [L3], $(Ax)_i=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t x_j$. Repeated application of [L5], by induction on the finite number of summands, distributes the products over these sums. Re-enumerating the resulting finite sum over pairs $(j,t)$ as $(t,j)$ is permitted by [L4]. For each fixed $t$, exactly the term $j=c_t$ survives, so the result is $\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}v_t x_{c_t}$. By step 1.1 this equals $y_i$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $m=0$, both $y$ and $Ax$ are the unique empty vector by [L6]. If $m>0$, step 2.1 gives equality in every coordinate $i<m$, hence $y=Ax$. [L6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The theorem counts stored slots and visits, retaining the additive constant when m=s=0 and reserving O(m+s) for m>=1. The O(s) consequence requires at least one stored entry per row. It is a finite arithmetic/storage count, with no interval endpoint, equivalence, or selection from an arbitrary family.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not
runtime, memory-bandwidth, convergence, or factorization-cost bounds.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The value, column-index, and row-pointer arrays have lengths $s$, $s$, and $m+1$, respectively, so their input representation contains exactly $2s+m+1$ data slots. [L1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: The value, column-index, and row-pointer arrays have lengths $s$, $s$, and $m+1$, respectively, so their input representation contains exactly $2s+m+1$ data slots.

Summing these lengths telescopes to $r_m-r_0=s$; monotonicity makes the intervals disjoint and their endpoints cover every stored index once. Thus the accumulation loop executes exactly $s$ multiply-add updates, and the initialization loop executes exactly $m$ times. The two validation scans examine at most $m+1$ pointers and $s$ column indices, so validation and loop control take $O(m+s+1)$ work. [L1, L3, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The returned vector occupies $m$ additional field slots. items.assessment: The Statement fixes a finite matrix/order and assumes each executed pivot nonzero. Its induction proves only numerical-support inclusion in the symbolic filled graph, expressly allowing cancellation and excluding a cost/equality conclusion. No interval endpoint or arbitrary choice is used; the elimination ordering is supplied, not selected by a choice axiom.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $F$ be a field, let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy $A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for
all $i,j<n$, and fix an elimination ordering,
and let $G_k=(V_k,E_k)$ be its symbolic filled graphs from
[[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]]. Put $S^0=A$.
Assume each pivot $p_k:=S^k_{v_kv_k}$ is nonzero, and for every pair of
remaining vertices define the Schur update

$$S^{k+1}_{ij}:=S^k_{ij}-\frac{S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}}{p_k}.$$

Then for every stage $k$, each nonzero off-diagonal entry $S^k_{ij}$ has
$\{i,j\}\in E_k$. At each elimination step, the later neighbors of the
eliminated vertex form a clique in the next filled graph. Thus the symbolic
filled graph contains the numerical Schur-complement support; equality is not
asserted.
claim_sections.Remarks: The conclusion is a support inclusion, not equality: an arithmetic subtraction can cancel a nonzero entry while the symbolic edge remains. The companion page gives an explicit cancellation calculation in [[ex-numerical-cancellation-within-filled-graph]]. No factorization-cost bound follows from this graph statement.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: At stage $0$, $S^0=A$ and the initial edge set consists exactly of the unordered off-diagonal pairs with nonzero matrix entry. Hence every nonzero off-diagonal entry of $S^0$ corresponds to an edge of $G_0$. [given, L1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: At stage $0$, $S^0=A$ and the initial edge set consists exactly of the unordered off-diagonal pairs with nonzero matrix entry. Hence every nonzero off-diagonal entry of $S^0$ corresponds to an edge of $G_0$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Suppose the support inclusion holds at stage $k$. If $S^{k+1}_{ij}\ne0$ for distinct $i,j\in V_{k+1}$, then at least one of $S^k_{ij}$ and $S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}/p_k$ is nonzero. In the first case, the induction hypothesis gives $\{i,j\}\in E_k$, and the update retains that edge. In the second case, the numerator is nonzero because a zero numerator would give a zero quotient by [L2] and [L3]; then [L4] forces both pivot couplings to be nonzero. The induction hypothesis gives $\{i,v_k\},\{v_k,j\}\in E_k$, so $i,j\in N_k(v_k)$ and the update adds $\{i,j\}$. Thus every such nonzero is supported by an edge of $G_{k+1}$. [A1, L1, L2, L3, L4, induction, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Suppose the support inclusion holds at stage $k$. If $S^{k+1}_{ij}\ne0$ for distinct $i,j\in V_{k+1}$, then at least one of $S^k_{ij}$ and $S^k_{iv_k}S^k_{v_kj}/p_k$ is nonzero. In the first case, the induction hypothesis gives $\{i,j\}\in E_k$, and the update retains that edge. In the second case, the numerator is nonzero because a zero numerator would give a zero quotient by [L2] and [L3]; then [L4] forces both pivot couplings to be nonzero. The induction hypothesis gives $\{i,v_k\},\{v_k,j\}\in E_k$, so $i,j\in N_k(v_k)$ and the update adds $\{i,j\}$. Thus every such nonzero is supported by an edge of $G_{k+1}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The base case and induction step prove the support inclusion at every stage. For any two distinct later neighbors of $v_k$, the graph update inserts their pair by definition, so the later-neighbor set is a clique in $G_{k+1}$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, induction] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: The base case and induction step prove the support inclusion at every stage. For any two distinct later neighbors of $v_k$, the graph update inserts their pair by definition, so the later-neighbor set is a clique in $G_{k+1}$.

$$\sum_{j<n}\sum_{k<n}a_{jk}=\sum_{k<n}\sum_{j<n}a_{jk}.$$

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, and let $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be the evaluation function of a formal real polynomial of degree at most $m$, or the zero polynomial. Write its actual coefficient list through its degree and extend that list by zeros to $a_0,\ldots,a_m$ (all zero for the zero polynomial); this is an evaluation vector, not a change to the formal polynomial object. Define iterated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]] and write $m!_{\mathbb R}:=\prod_{j<m}(j+1)$, with each natural factor read as its canonical real image under [[def-canonical-natural]]. Then
$$p^{(m)}(x)=a_m m!_{\mathbb R}$$
for every $x\in\mathbb R$. In particular, this derivative is zero if $\deg p<m$, and it is $m!_{\mathbb R}$ if $p$ is monic of degree $m$.
