claim_sections.Definition:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and let $u_0,\ldots,u_{n-1}\in\mathbb R$ and nonzero $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}\in\mathbb R$. For $d\ne0$, use $u/d$ to denote $u d^{-1}$. Then
$$\prod_{k<n}\frac{u_k}{d_k}=\frac{\prod_{k<n}u_k}{\prod_{k<n}d_k}.$$
The denominator on the right is nonzero by [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]]. The identity includes $n=0$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $n=0$, both products are empty and equal $1$ by [F1]. Also $1^{-1}=1$, since $1\cdot1=1$ and inverses are unique by [F3, F4]. Thus both sides equal $1$. [base, given, F1, F3, F4]

By [F5], both $D$ and the extended denominator product $Dd_n$ are nonzero, so $D^{-1}$ and $(Dd_n)^{-1}$ exist; also $d_n^{-1}$ exists by [F3]. Associativity and commutativity give $(Dd_n)(D^{-1}d_n^{-1})=(DD^{-1})(d_nd_n^{-1})=1$, so uniqueness [F4] gives $(Dd_n)^{-1}=D^{-1}d_n^{-1}$. Using the induction hypothesis, product recursion [F1], and the quotient convention, $$\prod_{k<n+1}\frac{u_k}{d_k}=\left(\prod_{k<n}\frac{u_k}{d_k}\right)\frac{u_n}{d_n}=\frac{U}{D}\frac{u_n}{d_n}=\frac{Uu_n}{Dd_n}=\frac{\prod_{k<n+1}u_k}{\prod_{k<n+1}d_k}.$$ The equality $(U/D)(u_n/d_n)=(Uu_n)/(Dd_n)$ follows from associativity and commutativity together with $(Dd_n)^{-1}=D^{-1}d_n^{-1}$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, ih, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $m\in\mathbb N$ with $m\ge6$, and take the $2m+1$ nodes
$$x_k=-1+\frac{k}{m},\qquad 0\le k\le2m.$$
They are equally spaced in $[-1,1]$. Let $\ell_m$ be the cardinal function for the node $x_m=0$, and set
$$x_*=-1+\frac{1}{2m}.$$
Then
$$|\ell_m(x_*)|\ge\frac{9\,m}{1280}.$$
In these real formulas, natural numbers and binomial coefficients denote their canonical real images, as specified by [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-binomial-coefficient]], and [[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]].

In the numerator, the $k=0$ factor is $1/2$ and the remaining factors are $k-1/2$ for $1\le k\le2m$, with $k=m$ omitted. Pairing the odd factors gives $\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le2m\\k\ne m}}|\tfrac12-k|=\frac{(4m)!_{\mathbb R}}{(2m-1)16^m(2m)!_{\mathbb R}}.$ Using [F3, F4] to rewrite the factorial ratios yields the exact identity $|\ell_m(x_*)|=\frac{\binom{4m}{2m}\,\binom{2m}{m}}{(2m-1)16^m}.$ [given, F1, F3, F4, F9, F11, algebra]

Consequently $\binom{4m}{2m}\ge\frac{16^m}{4m+1},\qquad \binom{2m}{m}\ge\frac{4^m}{2m+1}.$ [given, F2, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement: Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [F2], choose a formal polynomial $P$ of degree at most $n$ (allowing the zero polynomial) whose evaluation $p(t):=P(t)$ equals the function $I_n y(t)$ for every real $t$. At node $x_i$, [F1, F2] give $P(x_i)=p(x_i)=\sum_{j=0}^ny_j\ell_j(x_i)=y_i$. Thus the formal polynomial $P$ is an interpolant. [given, F1, F2, choose, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [F2], choose a formal polynomial $P$ of degree at most $n$ (allowing the zero polynomial) whose evaluation $p(t):=P(t)$ equals the function $I_n y(t)$ for every real $t$. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $Q$ be any formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ (allowing zero) with $Q(x_i)=y_i$, and denote its evaluation by $q(t):=Q(t)$. Extend the actual coefficient lists of $P$ and $Q$ by zeros through index $n$ (using all-zero vectors for zero polynomials), obtaining vectors $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$; these describe their evaluations $p$ and $q$, not padded formal objects. The vector $c_k=a_k-b_k$ defines by [F3] a formal polynomial $r$ of degree at most $n$; [F5] gives $r(t)=p(t)-q(t)$ for every real $t$. Since $p$ and $q$ agree at all nodes by step 1.1 and the choice of $q$, $r$ has the $n+1$ distinct roots $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. If $r$ were nonzero, [F4] would give at most $\deg r\le n$ roots, a contradiction. Hence $r$ is the zero formal polynomial; by [F3], every $a_k-b_k=0$. The canonical coefficient lists of $P$ and $Q$ are therefore identical (or both objects are zero), so $P=Q$, and consequently $p=q$ as evaluation functions. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, and define $\omega_n,w_j,I_n y$ as in [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. For every real $x$ that is not a node,
$$\omega_n(x)\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{w_j}{x-x_j}=1,\qquad \omega_n(x)\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{y_jw_j}{x-x_j}=I_n y(x).$$
In particular, the denominator sum is nonzero and
$$I_n y(x)=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_jw_j/(x-x_j)}{\sum_{j=0}^{n}w_j/(x-x_j)}.$$
At a node $x_i$, the interpolant is defined by the separate value $I_n y(x_i)=y_i$; the quotient is not used there.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Split the product for $\omega_n(x)$ before and after index $j$ using [F4]: it is $A(x-x_j)B$, where $A=\prod_{k<j}(x-x_k)$ and $B=\prod_{j<k\le n}(x-x_k)$. Since $x\ne x_j$, division by $x-x_j$ gives $AB=\prod_{k\ne j}(x-x_k)$ in the increasing omitted-index order of [F1]. Multiplying by $w_j$ therefore gives $\ell_j(x)=\omega_n(x)w_j/(x-x_j)$. [given, F1, F4, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Split the product for $\omega_n(x)$ before and after index $j$ using [F4]: it is $A(x-x_j)B$, where $A=\prod_{k<j}(x-x_k)$ and $B=\prod_{j<k\le n}(x-x_k)$. Since $x\ne x_j$, division by $x-x_j$ gives $AB=\prod_{k\ne j}(x-x_k)$ in the increasing omitted-index order of [F1]. Multiplying by $w_j$ therefore gives $\ell_j(x)=\omega_n(x)w_j/(x-x_j)$.

The constant polynomial $1$ is another degree-at-most-$n$ interpolant of these data; uniqueness in [F2] gives $S(X)=1$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

Since $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ by [F3], the denominator sum equals $1/\omega_n(x)$ and is nonzero by the field laws [F4]. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Dividing this identity by the nonzero identity in step 2.1 proves the quotient formula. At $x_i$, [F2] gives $I_n y(x_i)=y_i$, which is the separate node value stated above. claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $a<b$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ lie in $[a,b]$, and let $f\in C^{n+1}([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with the convention of [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Put $p=I_n f$ and $\omega_n(X)=\prod_{j=0}^n(X-x_j)$ as in [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. If $x=x_j$ for a node, then $f(x)-p(x)=0$. If $x\in[a,b]$ is not a node, there is
$$\xi\in\bigl(\min\{x,x_0\},\max\{x,x_n\}\bigr)$$
such that
$$f(x)-p(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}}\,\omega_n(x),$$
where $(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}:=\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}j$, with each natural factor read as its canonical real image under [[def-canonical-natural]].

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Suppose $x$ is not a node. By [F8], $\omega_n(x)\ne0$, so set $c=(f(x)-p(x))/\omega_n(x)$ and define $g(t)=f(t)-p(t)-c\omega_n(t)$ on $[a,b]$. At every node $x_j$, [F2] gives $f(x_j)=p(x_j)$ and [F1] gives $\omega_n(x_j)=0$, so $g(x_j)=0$; by the choice of $c$, also $g(x)=0$. [given, F1, F2, F8, construct]

items.assessment: The Definition supplies finite arrays and fixed index order. It validates nodes/data, returns an exact node value before testing representable one, and otherwise guards every weight/quotient operation. No maximizer or witness is selected from a family; matching a unique strictly ordered node is a finite deterministic test.

claim_sections.Definition:
The input is a natural number $n\ge0$, a floating-point system $(\mathbb F,N_{\min},N_{\max},\operatorname{fl})$ satisfying [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]], a node array of exactly $n+1$ candidates $x_0,\ldots,x_n$, a data array of exactly $n+1$ values $y_0,\ldots,y_n$, and a query $x$. The output is either a record with status *success* and a value in $\mathbb F$, or one of the statuses *invalid_nodes*, *invalid_data*, and *range_failure*.

Use checked operations as follows. For $a,b\in\mathbb F$ and $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, return *range_failure* if division has $b=0$ or if the exact real result $a\circ b$ is nonzero and outside the normal range $N_{\min}\le|a\circ b|\le N_{\max}$. Otherwise return $\operatorname{fl}(a\circ b)$, using the exact-zero rule when the result is zero. Each checked operation has the tagged outcome either *range_failure* or a value in $\mathbb F$; if an operation in a displayed sequence returns *range_failure*, stop before evaluating the next operation and return that status. Thus $\operatorname{fl}$ is called only on arguments in the domain of the stated model.

Procedure:

1. If the node array has length other than $n+1$, any node is not in $\mathbb F$, or the nodes are not strictly increasing, return *invalid_nodes*. If the data array has length other than $n+1$, or any data value or the query is not in $\mathbb F$, return *invalid_data*.
2. If $x=x_i$ for some $i$, return *success* with value $y_i$.
3. If $1\notin\mathbb F$, return *range_failure*. Otherwise, for each $j=0,\ldots,n$, initialize $d_j=1$. For each $k=0,\ldots,n$ with $k\ne j$, compute $\delta=\operatorname{checked}_{-}(x_j,x_k)$ and then replace $d_j$ by $\operatorname{checked}_{\times}(d_j,\delta)$. After this inner loop set $w_j=\operatorname{checked}_{\div}(1,d_j)$. Any checked-operation failure returns *range_failure*.
4. Initialize $N=0$ and $D=0$. For each $j=0,\ldots,n$, compute $\delta_j=\operatorname{checked}_{-}(x,x_j)$, $u_j=\operatorname{checked}_{\div}(\operatorname{checked}_{\times}(w_j,y_j),\delta_j)$, and $v_j=\operatorname{checked}_{\div}(w_j,\delta_j)$. Replace $N$ by $\operatorname{checked}_{+}(N,u_j)$ and $D$ by $\operatorname{checked}_{+}(D,v_j)$. Any checked-operation failure returns *range_failure*.
5. If $D=0$, return *range_failure*. Otherwise return *success* with value $\operatorname{checked}_{\div}(N,D)$, unless that final checked operation returns *range_failure*.

The exact-arithmetic target of steps 3–5 is the quotient in [[thm-barycentric-interpolation-identities]]. This finite-arithmetic procedure provides no forward-error bound, conditioning guarantee, or accuracy certificate; close or widely separated nodes can cause a range failure or an inaccurate successful value.

items.assessment: This binary-grid lemma fixes precision at least two with unbounded exponents. Its proof constructs each binade by a finite bounded integer search, handles zero operands separately, and proves ordered cancellation through representable grid differences. The four one-way grid properties are not a biconditional or a selection from an arbitrary family.

claim_sections.Statement:
For an integer $p\ge2$, let $\mathbb B_p=\{0\}\cup\{\pm m2^k: m,k\in\mathbb Z,\ 2^{p-1}\le m<2^p\}$, with unbounded exponent. Let $R$ round a real number to its nearest member of $\mathbb B_p$, breaking ties by the even normalized significand; set $R(0)=0$. For $x\ne0$ put $E(x)$ be the unique integer with $2^{E(x)}\le|x|<2^{E(x)+1}$, and set $q(x)=2^{E(x)-p+1}$. The following hold.

- $R$ is monotone, odd, and fixes $\mathbb B_p$. For $R(t)\ne0$, $|R(t)-t|\le q(R(t))/2$.
- If $x,y\in\mathbb B_p$, then $\rho=R(x+y)-(x+y)$ belongs to $\mathbb B_p$ and $|\rho|\le\min(|x|,|y|)$. If $|R(x+y)|<\min(|x|,|y|)$, the sum is exact.
- If $x,y\in\mathbb B_p$ have the same sign and $|x|/2\le|y|\le2|x|$, then $x-y\in\mathbb B_p$ (Sterbenz exact subtraction).
- If $A,B\in\mathbb B_p$ and $|A|\ge|B|$, then $S=R(A+B)$, $Z=R(S-A)$, $T=R(B-Z)$ satisfy $Z=S-A$ and $T=A+B-S$ exactly.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Integer induction gives $2^n\ge n+1$ for $n\ge0$: the initial equality is immediate and $2^{n+1}\ge2(n+1)\ge n+2$. For $t>0$, [F1] supplies a natural $N>\max(t,1/t,1)$, so $2^{-N}<t<2^N$. The finite set of integers $j\in[-N,N]$ with $2^j\le t$ is nonempty and has a largest element $E$; it satisfies $2^E\le t<2^{E+1}$. Strict increase of powers of two makes $E$ unique. Thus the stated $E(x)$ exists for every $x\ne0$. In its binade, the finitely many points $m2^{E-p+1}$, $2^{p-1}\le m\le2^p$, bracket $t$; their adjacent neighbors determine its nearest point. Points outside that bracket cannot be nearer, and zero is farther than a positive grid point; negative arguments follow by reflection. On a binade $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$, the nonnegative grid has spacing $2^{j-p+1}$. Its consecutive midpoints partition the real line into nearest-point cells, proving monotonicity and exactness on the grid; reflection preserves the even-significand tie rule, proving oddness. Every nonzero real number has two bracketing grid points, so a nearest point exists and is nonzero for a nonzero argument. The gaps on either side of a grid point $c\ne0$ are at most $q(c)$, including the half-sized lower gap at a power of two. Its rounding cell therefore gives $|R(t)-t|\le q(R(t))/2$. Also, for any power of two $h$, every integer multiple $nh$ with $|n|\le2^p$ is in $\mathbb B_p$: the integer has at most $p$ significant bits, except $|n|=2^p$, which is a power of two. [given, F1, algebra]

items.assessment: The Statement includes zero operands, exact cancellation and successful calls at both normal-range endpoints. the proof transfers finite-range success to unbounded binary rounding; later magnitude/sign branches prove the residual identity. Precision at least two and the no-underflow success policy stay explicit; no arbitrary choice is introduced.

claim_sections.Statement:
Use a binary floating-point format of precision $p\ge2$: its normal positive values are $m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $e_{\min}\le j\le e_{\max}$, with their negatives and zero. Any additional representable values below the normal range must belong to the unbounded binary set $\mathbb B_p$ of [[lem-binary-rounding-grid-and-ordered-two-sum]] (as ordinary binary subnormals do). Round each operation to nearest, ties to even, with the no-underflow success rule of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]].

For any representable real inputs $a,b$ for which [[alg-two-sum-error-free-transform]] succeeds, its output satisfies
$$s=\operatorname{fl}(a+b),\qquad e=(a+b)-s,\qquad s+e=a+b$$
exactly in real arithmetic. No ordering or sign condition on the inputs is required; zeros, exact cancellation, and all successful calls at either normal-range boundary are included.
claim_sections.Remarks: The binary digit hypothesis supplies exactness information absent from the relative-error model alone. Shewchuk's Theorem 7 states the binary result for $p\ge3$; step 3.1 uses the sharper bound on $s-a$ directly to include $p=2$ as well. The theorem retains unrestricted inputs and does not assume that the residual operations are exact: their exactness is proved above.

complete metric space $\mathbb R$ with distance $d(u,v)=|u-v|$. The remaining

$H(x)=(x-1)^2$.

claim_sections.Statement:
If $a<b$ in a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every relative open cover of
$[a,b]$ has a finite subcover. Relative openness means openness in the
subspace topology inherited from the real line.

A member containing $a$ contains a relative neighborhood $[a,a+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$; choosing $\eta=\min(\delta/2,(b-a)/2)$ shows $a+\eta\in S$. Thus $S$ is nonempty and bounded above by $b$. By [A1], $c=\sup S$ exists. [given, A1, construct]

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$

Its Statement and final argument separately cover reversed endpoints and zero-length intervals with both sides zero. claim_sections.Statement:
Let $f,g$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$.
Then $\alpha f+\beta g$ is continuous and
$$\int_a^b(\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t))\,dt =\alpha\int_a^b f(t)\,dt+\beta\int_a^b g(t)\,dt.$$
The same identity holds for the oriented integral when $b<a$, and for the
zero-length interval both sides are zero.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: On each partition interval, the maximum of $f+g$ is at most the sum of the separate maxima, while its minimum is at least the sum of the separate minima. Thus $U(f+g,P)\le U(f,P)+U(g,P)$ and $L(f+g,P)\ge L(f,P)+L(g,P)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose partitions whose upper sums for $f,g$ are within $\varepsilon/2$ above their infima, and refine both to a common partition $P$. By [L1], refinement cannot increase those upper sums, so $\int_a^b(f+g)\le U(f+g,P)<\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g+\varepsilon$. Similarly choose lower sums within $\varepsilon/2$ below their suprema and refine to a common partition; [L1] gives $\int_a^b(f+g)\ge L(f+g,P)>\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g-\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, the integral is additive in the integrand. [given, L1, choose, construct, algebra]

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose partitions whose upper sums for $f,g$ are within $\varepsilon/2$ above their infima, and refine both to a common partition $P$. By [L1], refinement cannot increase those upper sums, so $\int_a^b(f+g)\le U(f+g,P)<\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g+\varepsilon$. Similarly choose lower sums within $\varepsilon/2$ below their suprema and refine to a common partition; [L1] gives $\int_a^b(f+g)\ge L(f+g,P)>\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g-\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, the integral is additive in the integrand.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: If $\alpha>0$, maxima and minima of $\alpha f$ on every partition piece are $\alpha$ times those of $f$, so both Darboux sums scale by $\alpha$ and their infimum/supremum do as well. If $\alpha=0$, every sum is zero. If $\alpha<0$, multiplication reverses order, giving $U(\alpha f,P)=\alpha L(f,P)$ and $L(\alpha f,P)=\alpha U(f,P)$; taking the infimum and supremum, which reverse under multiplication by negative $\alpha$, again gives $\int_a^b\alpha f=\alpha\int_a^b f$. Combine this homogeneity with step 1.1 to obtain the displayed formula. For reversed endpoints use $\int_b^a=-\int_a^b$; for $a=b$ use the zero-length definition. [given, L1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The Statement requires n>=1 and a nonzero increment in every input coordinate, so its component sum and maximum index sets are nonempty. The proof divides only by the prescribed nonzero h_i and combines the componentwise remainder bounds by Cauchy-Schwarz. This is a specified coordinate stencil, not an empty-dimensional or zero-step claim.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let each component
$F_j:U\to\mathbb R$, $j<n$, be $C^2$ (twice continuously differentiable). Fix
$x\in U$ and increments $h=(h_0,\ldots,h_{n-1})\in\mathbb R^n$ with $h_i\ne0$
for every $i<n$. For each $i<n$, suppose an open interval
$I_i\subseteq\mathbb R$ contains $[0,1]$ and $x+t h_i e_i\in U$ for every
$t\in I_i$. Suppose finite constants $M_{ij}\ge0$ satisfy
$$|\partial_{ii}F_j(x+t h_i e_i)|\le M_{ij}\qquad(0\le t\le1,\ j<n).$$
Put $M_i:=(\sum_{j<n}M_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$ and $M:=\max_{i<n}M_i$.
Let $J_hF(x)$ be the forward-difference matrix of
[[alg-forward-difference-jacobian]], let $J_F(x)$ be the Jacobian matrix of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. With the
Euclidean operator norm on matrices,
$$\|J_hF(x)-J_F(x)\|_{\rm op}\le\frac M2\|h\|_2.$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: By [F7], the $C^2$ components and their first partials have the total derivatives needed for the chain rule, and $F$ is admissible for [F1]. For each input coordinate $i<n$ and output component $j<n$, put $g_{ij}(t):=F_j(x+t h_i e_i)$ on $I_i$. The chain rule [F4] and Jacobian identification [F3] give $g_{ij}'(t)=h_i\partial_iF_j(x+t h_i e_i)$ and $g_{ij}''(t)=h_i^2\partial_{ii}F_j(x+t h_i e_i)$. Taylor's theorem [F5] between $0$ and $1$ supplies $\theta_{ij}\in(0,1)$ with $F_j(x+h_i e_i)-F_j(x)=h_i\partial_iF_j(x)+\frac{h_i^2}{2}\partial_{ii}F_j(x+\theta_{ij}h_i e_i)$. The points $\theta_{ij}$ may differ between components. [given, F3, F4, F5, F7, choose]

items.assessment: The Definition fixes d>=1 and positive steps. Its word family refers to prescribed step maps, not an aggregate that needs an empty-family value; the uniform-order hypothesis is conditional on admitted solution segments and stages in K. No existence of such a method or estimate outside those admitted inputs is asserted.

claim_sections.Definition:
Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

items.assessment: The Statement requires d>=1 and a nondegenerate time interval containing an actual solution graph. Its component sums run over one through d, and its proof composes the supplied solution with the given vector field. Thus no empty component family occurs; zero bounds or vector-field components remain admitted in the one-way derivative estimate.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and let $y:I\to\mathbb R^d$ solve $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open interval $I$. Fix $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subset I$ such that $(s,y(s))\in V$ for every $s\in[a,b]$. Suppose finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij}\ge0$ satisfy for all $s\in[a,b]$

$$|f_j(s,y(s))|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))|\le M_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$

Define $g_i(s):=f_i(s,y(s))$ and $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$. Then $g_i$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and

$$g_i'(s)=\partial_t f_i(s,y(s))+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{z_j}f_i(s,y(s))f_j(s,y(s)),\qquad |g_i'(s)|\le B_i.$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: By [F2]–[F3], $f$ is continuous on $V$. Since $y'=f(s,y(s))$, the derivative of $y$ is continuous on $I$; hence $y$ is continuously differentiable and the path $q(s):=(s,y(s))$ has derivative $q'(s)=(1,f(s,y(s)))$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For each $i$, the component map $f_i$ is totally differentiable, so [F4] applied to $g_i=f_i\circ q$ gives the displayed derivative formula. The bounds give $|g_i'(s)|\le M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j=B_i$ for every $s\in(a,b)$. Continuity of $g_i$ on $[a,b]$ follows from continuity of $f$ and $y$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The Statement requires positive state dimension and horizon and an actual solution graph in K, excluding an empty compact domain for this instance. The finite sums of component bounds are nonempty; the proof separately handles zero elapsed integration variable and derives local Euler defect/stability only for admitted positive steps. It claims no global error estimate.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be an open time-state domain whose fibers $V_t:=\{z:(t,z)\in V\}$ are open and convex. Let $K\subset V$ be compact. Let $f:V\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and suppose $y$ is a solution of $y'=f(t,y)$, $y(0)=y_0$, on an open interval containing $[0,T]$, with graph on $[0,T]$ contained in $K$. For each local defect under consideration, require the Euler input and output time-state pairs to lie in $K$; the exact solution segment already lies in $K$.

For $1\le i,j\le d$, assume finite constants $F_j,M_{t,i},M_{ij},L\ge0$ satisfy throughout $V$

$$|f_j(t,z)|\le F_j,\qquad |\partial_t f_i(t,z)|\le M_{t,i},\qquad |\partial_{z_j}f_i(t,z)|\le M_{ij},\qquad \|D_yf(t,z)w\|_2\le L\|w\|_2\quad(w\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Here $D_yf$ is the matrix with entries $\partial_{z_j}f_i$, and the last inequality defines the operator bound used below. The forward Euler map is $\Psi_h(t,v)=v+h f(t,v)$. Then, with $B_i:=M_{t,i}+\sum_{j=1}^dM_{ij}F_j$, for every $t\in[0,T)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$ whose Euler input and output pairs lie in $K$, its local defect satisfies

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le \frac{h^2}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^d B_i^2\right)^{1/2},$$

so it has uniform local order one on $K$ along $y|_{[0,T]}$, with $h_0=T$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, every admitted $h>0$, and every $u,v\in V_t$,

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2.$$

This is a local defect and one-step stability result. It does not assert a global error estimate or an order for any other named method.
claim_sections.Remarks: The defect proof is choice-free and uses only the time-along-flow chain rule and the componentwise integral remainder. The Taylor supplier is used by the scalar linear example, not needed to prove this theorem. The global error recurrence in the cited numerical-analysis sources is outside this item.

On each open convex fiber $V_t$, the derivative bound and [F5]–[F6] make $f(t,\cdot)$ $L$-Lipschitz. Thus the hypotheses of [F7] hold and the IVP has a unique maximal solution; the given solution agrees with it throughout $[0,T]$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7]

items.assessment: The Statement requires L,N>=1 and deterministic B0 through BL>=1. Its proof includes initialization, conditional event second moments, the a=0 branch without division and the zero-normalizer fallback branch. At B0=1 the initial factor is one; the product bound is a sufficient implication, not a consequence of mean-only deterministic-target bounds.

claim_sections.Statement:
Use the full-multinomial-resampling event model of [[alg-fixed-level-sir-splitting]] with $L\ge1$, $N\ge1$ and positive prefix normalizers. Put $Z=Z_L=P(A_L)>0$, define $q_L=1$ and $q_{p-1}=M_p(G_pq_p)$ for $1\le p\le L$, and let $\eta_p^N$ denote the weighted empirical state law after selection at level $p$. Suppose deterministic finite constants $B_0,\ldots,B_L\ge1$ satisfy $P(q_0^2)\le B_0Z^2$ and, almost surely on $\{\widehat Z_{p-1}>0\}$,
$$\eta_{p-1}^NM_p[(G_pq_p)^2]\le B_p\{\eta_{p-1}^NM_p(G_pq_p)\}^2,\qquad1\le p\le L.$$
Then
$$\mathbb E[(\widehat Z_L-Z)^2]\le Z^2\left\{\prod_{p=0}^L\left(1+\frac{B_p-1}{N}\right)-1\right\}.$$
If $B_0=1$ and $B_p\le B$ for $1\le p\le L$, this is at most $Z^2[(1+(B-1)/N)^L-1]$. The conditions involve actual conditional event second moments under random empirical predictive laws. Bounds on squared conditional future means under the deterministic target laws alone do not imply them.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Write $\alpha_p=1+(B_p-1)/N$. The initial particles are IID from $P$, $\widehat Z_0=1$ and $G_0=1$, so $U_0=N^{-1}\sum_iq_0(X_0^i)$ has mean $Z$ and second moment $Z^2+[P(q_0^2)-Z^2]/N\le\alpha_0Z^2$. All $U_p$ lie in $[0,1]$ by [F2], so all following conditional second moments exist. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

The initial particles are IID from $P$, $\widehat Z_0=1$ and $G_0=1$, so $U_0=N^{-1}\sum_iq_0(X_0^i)$ has mean $Z$ and second moment $Z^2+[P(q_0^2)-Z^2]/N\le\alpha_0Z^2$. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Conditional on the particle history $\mathcal F_{p-1}$, put $z=\widehat Z_{p-1}$, $a=\eta_{p-1}^NM_p(G_pq_p)$ and $b=\eta_{p-1}^NM_p[(G_pq_p)^2]$. If $z=0$, the zero-normalizer branch makes $U_p=U_{p-1}=0$, so the inequality also holds without a hypothesis on the fallback empirical law. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

By [F1] and [F3], $\mathbb E[U_p^2\mid\mathcal F_{p-1}]=z^2[a^2+(b-a^2)/N]$. On $z>0$, the hypothesis $b\le B_pa^2$ bounds this by $\alpha_p z^2a^2=\alpha_pU_{p-1}^2$, using $q_{p-1}=M_p(G_pq_p)$. If $z=0$, the zero-normalizer branch makes $U_p=U_{p-1}=0$, so the inequality also holds without a hypothesis on the fallback empirical law.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Taking expectations in step 1.2 and iterating over $p=1,\ldots,L$ yields $\mathbb EU_L^2\le\prod_{p=1}^L\alpha_p\,\mathbb EU_0^2\le Z^2\prod_{p=0}^L\alpha_p$. If $B_0=1$ then $\alpha_0=1$; if every remaining $B_p\le B$, each remaining factor is at most $1+(B-1)/N$, giving the specialization. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3, F4, algebra, induction] ∎

items.assessment: The Statement requires a positive bit budget, so its prefix sum has at least one bit; the underlying countable fair-bit sequence is also nonempty. The proof constructs the same-stream midpoint coupling, handles closed uniform endpoints through its CDF, and distinguishes the atomic grid by total variation one. It uses the declared Countable/Dependent Choice suppliers only.

claim_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice as in [[thm-independent-fair-bit-streams-produce-uniforms]]. Let $U=\sum_{j\ge1}B_j2^{-j}$ be the uniform variable from an independent fair-bit stream. For $b\ge1$, put
$$K_b=\sum_{j=1}^b B_j2^{b-j},\qquad U_b=(K_b+1/2)2^{-b},\qquad \delta_b=2^{-b-1}.$$
Then $K_b$ is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}$, $|U-U_b|\le\delta_b$ pointwise, the 1-Wasserstein and Kolmogorov distances between their laws are at most $\delta_b$, and their total-variation distance is exactly $1$. We use $W_1(\mu,
u)=\inf\mathbb E|X-Y|$ over couplings, $d_K(\mu,
u)=\sup_x|F_\mu(x)-F_
u(x)|$, and $d_{m TV}(\mu,
u)=\sup_A|\mu(A)-
u(A)|$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The first $b$ independent fair bits give each of the $2^b$ binary prefixes probability $2^{-b}$, so $K_b$ is uniform on the stated integer set. Write the remaining binary tail as $T_b=\sum_{j\ge1}B_{b+j}2^{-j}\in[0,1]$. Then $U=K_b2^{-b}+2^{-b}T_b$, while $U_b=K_b2^{-b}+2^{-b-1}$, hence $|U-U_b|=2^{-b}|T_b-1/2|\le2^{-b-1}$. [given, F1, A2, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: The first $b$ independent fair bits give each of the $2^b$ binary prefixes probability $2^{-b}$, so $K_b$ is uniform on the stated integer set. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The displayed coupling gives $W_1(\mathcal L(U),\mathcal L(U_b))\le\mathbb E|U-U_b|\le\delta_b$ by the infimum definition of $W_1$. For non-strict CDFs, $\{U\le x-\delta_b\}\subseteq\{U_b\le x\}\subseteq\{U\le x+\delta_b\}$; for strict CDFs, $\{U<x-\delta_b\}\subseteq\{U_b<x\}\subseteq\{U<x+\delta_b\}$. Since both uniform CDFs equal the clipped identity by [A1], these inclusions bound each absolute discrepancy by $\delta_b$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, A1, algebra]

By [F2], this event gives $d_{\rm TV}(\mathcal L(U),\mathcal L(U_b))=1$, the maximal possible value. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

items.assessment: The Definition explicitly requires a nonempty outcome list and a probability sum one. It handles input zero by returning outcome one, then searches deterministically for the least cumulative threshold; r=1 needs no comparisons. No empty probability vector or unprescribed inverse choice is admitted by this algorithm.

claim_sections.Definition:
Input a nonempty finite list of outcomes $1,\ldots,r$ ($r\ge1$) with probabilities $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^r p_i=1$, and either an ideal bit-stream uniform $U\in[0,1]$ as in [[thm-independent-fair-bit-streams-produce-uniforms]] or a $b$-bit midpoint $U_b\in(0,1)$ as in [[thm-midpoint-bit-stream-coupling-and-error]]. Write $v$ for the supplied input. Let $C_0=0$ and $C_i=\sum_{j=1}^i p_j$.

1. If $v=0$, return outcome $1$. This assigns the ideal uniform's null zero-endpoint event an explicit value.
2. Otherwise initialize integer bounds $L=1$, $H=r$. While $L<H$, set $j=\lfloor(L+H)/2\rfloor$. If $v\le C_j$, set $H=j$; otherwise set $L=j+1$.
3. When $L=H$, return outcome $L$.

Thus on positive inputs the intended output is the least index with $v\le C_i$, including equality at a cumulative threshold. For ideal positive $U$, this is the generalized inverse of the step CDF $F(i)=C_i$ by [[lem-generalized-inverse-sublevel-identity]]. The midpoint and ideal-input law and binary-search properties are proved separately.
claim_sections.Remarks: With ideal $U$, this is exact finite categorical inversion. Midpoint input has a discrete law; its threshold counts, rather than total-variation closeness to a continuous uniform law, control its categorical error.

items.assessment: The Definition explicitly stipulates represented-set inclusion S sqsubseteq T exactly as set inclusion, so both directions are the defining condition, not unproved theorems. It separately names empty/entire/error statuses, admits singleton intervals and zero-radius balls, and excludes zero from complex reciprocal division.

claim_sections.Definition:
A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

items.assessment: The Definition assumes a supplied interval with a center c in it and integer n>=0, so its coefficient family has n+1>=1 entries. Zero width gives zero radius remainder, and n=0 still has a constant coefficient. Required derivative/coefficient enclosures are inputs and unavailable ones return no certificate, rather than being chosen implicitly.

claim_sections.Definition:
Let $f$ be a real function that is $n+1$ times continuously differentiable on
an open interval containing the finite real interval $X=[a,b]$. Here
$n\ge0$ is an integer, and continuous differentiability means that the
derivatives through order $n+1$ exist there and are continuous. Let $c\in X$
be a dyadic point. Put
$$
P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(t-c)^j.
$$
Supply dyadic intervals $C_j$ containing $f^{(j)}(c)/j!$ for $0\le j\le n$
and a dyadic interval $D$ containing $f^{(n+1)}(X)$. Put
$M=\max(|\inf D|,|\sup D|)$ and
$R=\max(|a-c|,|b-c|)$. The **centered Taylor-model enclosure** is
$$\mathcal T_n(f,X,c,(C_j)_{j=0}^n,D) =\sum_{j=0}^n C_j(X-c)^j+ \left[-\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\frac{M R^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\right],$$
where products, powers, sums, and the final sum are evaluated by
outward-rounded interval operations. The first term carries input variation
through the polynomial; the symmetric second interval is the explicit
derivative-based remainder. If a required coefficient or derivative
enclosure is unavailable, no Taylor-model certificate is returned.

items.assessment: The infinite coefficient sequences are indexed by all nonnegative integers, not an optional empty family. Each convolution sum includes j=0 through n, and finite partial sums have at least the zeroth term. The proof allows zero coefficient sequences and uses actual absolute-convergence bounds and tails; no separate empty-index aggregate is claimed.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n=A$ and $\sum_{n\ge0}b_n=B$ be absolutely convergent
real series. Define
$$
c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jb_{n-j}.
$$
Then $\sum_{n\ge0}c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. Thus the
product of the two series can be grouped by total degree without changing
its sum.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Put $A_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|$ and $B_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|b_n|$. For every $N$, the finite triangle inequality and [L1] give $$\sum_{n=0}^N|c_n| \le\sum_{j+\ell\le N}|a_j||b_\ell| \le\left(\sum_{j=0}^N|a_j|\right) \left(\sum_{\ell=0}^N|b_\ell|\right) \le A_0B_0.$$ These partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their supremum $S$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds $S-\varepsilon$, since otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound; monotonicity then puts every later partial sum between $S-\varepsilon$ and $S$. Hence $\sum c_n$ converges absolutely. [given, F1, L1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Put $A_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|$ and $B_0=\sum_{n\ge0}|b_n|$. For every $N$, the finite triangle inequality and [L1] give $$\sum_{n=0}^N|c_n| \le\sum_{j+\ell\le N}|a_j||b_\ell| \le\left(\sum_{j=0}^N|a_j|\right) \left(\sum_{\ell=0}^N|b_\ell|\right) \le A_0B_0.$$ These partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their supremum $S$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds $S-\varepsilon$, since otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound; monotonicity then puts every later partial sum between $S-\varepsilon$ and $S$. Hence $\sum c_n$ converges absolutely.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $A_N=\sum_{j=0}^N a_j$, $B_N=\sum_{\ell=0}^N b_\ell$, and $C_N=\sum_{n=0}^N c_n=\sum_{j+\ell\le N}a_jb_\ell$. The difference $A_NB_N-C_N$ is the sum over pairs $0\le j,\ell\le N$ with $j+\ell>N$. For each such pair, $j>N/2$ or $\ell>N/2$, so by [L1] $$|A_NB_N-C_N| \le B_0\sum_{j>N/2}|a_j|+A_0\sum_{\ell>N/2}|b_\ell|\longrightarrow0.$$ Absolute convergence makes both tails tend to zero. The convergent sequence $A_N$ is bounded: beyond some index $|A_N-A|<1$, and the finitely many earlier values have a finite maximum absolute value. Therefore $$ |A_NB_N-AB|\le |A_N||B_N-B|+|B||A_N-A|\longrightarrow0. $$ Together with $|A_NB_N-C_N|\to0$, this gives $C_N\to AB$. Thus the sum of the Cauchy product is $AB$, proving the claim. [given, L1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Let $A_N=\sum_{j=0}^N a_j$, $B_N=\sum_{\ell=0}^N b_\ell$, and $C_N=\sum_{n=0}^N c_n=\sum_{j+\ell\le N}a_jb_\ell$. items.assessment: Every stated series is indexed by a nonempty natural-number sequence; finite partial sums include their zeroth term. The proof explicitly separates R=0 and q=0 from positive ratio estimates and then uses bounded nonnegative partial sums. It asserts uniform convergence on bounded intervals, not a definition of a sum over an absent coefficient family.

claim_sections.Statement:
For every real $R\ge0$, the factorial series
$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n/n!$ converges. If $N\ge0$ and
$q=R/(N+2)<1$, its tail after index $N$ satisfies
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{R^n}{n!} \le \frac{R^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-q)}.$$
Consequently the series defining $\exp x$, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and each of
their formal derivative series converge absolutely and uniformly on every
bounded interval $|x|\le R$. For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series and the
odd power series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$, with their formal derivative
series, converge absolutely and uniformly on $|x|\le r$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $0\le q<1$. For every integer $m\ge0$, $(1-q)\sum_{k=0}^m q^k=1-q^{m+1}$. If $q=0$, its powers after the zeroth are zero. If $0<q<1$, then $1/q=1+d$ for $d>0$, and induction gives $(1+d)^m\ge1+md$. By [L1], $1+md$ is unbounded, so $0\le q^m\le1/(1+md)\to0$. Thus the geometric partial sums converge to $1/(1-q)$, with tail $q^{m+1}/(1-q)$. [given, L1, algebra, induction]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Let $0\le q<1$. For every integer $m\ge0$, $(1-q)\sum_{k=0}^m q^k=1-q^{m+1}$. If $q=0$, its powers after the zeroth are zero. If $0<q<1$, then $1/q=1+d$ for $d>0$, and induction gives $(1+d)^m\ge1+md$. By [L1], $1+md$ is unbounded, so $0\le q^m\le1/(1+md)\to0$. Thus the geometric partial sums converge to $1/(1-q)$, with tail $q^{m+1}/(1-q)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $R=0$ the factorial series is $1$. For $R>0$, choose $N$ with $q=R/(N+2)<1$ by [L1]. If $u_n=R^n/n!$, then for $n\ge N+1$, $u_{n+1}/u_n=R/(n+1)\le q$. Every finite tail after $N$ is therefore at most $u_{N+1}\sum_{j\ge0}q^j=u_{N+1}/(1-q)$ by step 1.1. The positive partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their supremum $S$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds $S-\varepsilon$, since otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound; monotonicity then puts all later partial sums between $S-\varepsilon$ and $S$. The finite-tail geometric bound passes to this limit and proves the stated estimate. [given, F1, L1, step 1.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For $R=0$ the factorial series is $1$. For $R>0$, choose $N$ with $q=R/(N+2)<1$ by [L1]. If $u_n=R^n/n!$, then for $n\ge N+1$, $u_{n+1}/u_n=R/(n+1)\le q$. Every finite tail after $N$ is therefore at most $u_{N+1}\sum_{j\ge0}q^j=u_{N+1}/(1-q)$ by step 1.1. The positive partial sums are increasing and bounded, so [F1] gives their supremum $S$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, some partial sum exceeds $S-\varepsilon$, since otherwise $S-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound; monotonicity then puts all later partial sums between $S-\varepsilon$ and $S$. The finite-tail geometric bound passes to this limit and proves the stated estimate.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $|x|\le R$, [L2] gives $|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!$. Thus the exponential series is uniformly Cauchy by the tail bound in step 2.1. The sine and cosine series are subseries of this same nonnegative majorant, so their absolute tails are uniform as well. For the formal derivative series, the exponential terms are bounded by $R^{n-1}/(n-1)!$; sine derivatives are bounded by $R^{2k}/(2k)!$, and nonconstant cosine derivatives by $R^{2k-1}/(2k-1)!$. Each is a subseries of a factorial series from step 2.1. The same tail comparison proves absolute and uniform convergence of all stated series. [L2, step 2.1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For $|x|\le R$, [L2] gives $|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!$. Thus the exponential series is uniformly Cauchy by the tail bound in step 2.1. The sine and cosine series are subseries of this same nonnegative majorant, so their absolute tails are uniform as well. For the formal derivative series, the exponential terms are bounded by $R^{n-1}/(n-1)!$; sine derivatives are bounded by $R^{2k}/(2k)!$, and nonconstant cosine derivatives by $R^{2k-1}/(2k-1)!$. Each is a subseries of a factorial series from step 2.1. The same tail comparison proves absolute and uniform convergence of all stated series.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $0\le r<1$, the absolute terms of $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ are bounded by $r^{2k+1}$ and the derivative terms by $r^{2k}$. Their tails converge uniformly by step 1.1 applied to $q=r^2$; multiplication by the fixed factor $r$ or $2$ does not affect convergence. This proves the assertions for the odd power series and its formal derivative series. [L2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For $0\le r<1$, the absolute terms of $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ are bounded by $r^{2k+1}$ and the derivative terms by $r^{2k}$. Their tails converge uniformly by step 1.1 applied to $q=r^2$; multiplication by the fixed factor $r$ or $2$ does not affect convergence. This proves the assertions for the odd power series and its formal derivative series.

items.assessment: The coefficient sequence starts at zero and the derivative sequence at one, both nonempty fixed index sets. The proof chooses one radius strictly between a fixed interior point and the positive convergence radius, then controls the two tails around finite polynomials. It does not require or assert differentiation of an unspecified empty series family.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $R_0>0$ and let $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ be real coefficients such that for every
$0<R<R_0$ both $\sum_{n\ge0}|a_n|R^n$ and
$\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$ converge. Then
$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is differentiable for $|x|<R_0$, with
$F'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}na_nx^{n-1}$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $c$ with $|c|<R_0$ and choose $R$ with $|c|<R<R_0$. For $0<|h|<R-|c|$, the identity $$ (c+h)^n-c^n=h\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j $$ for $n\ge1$ and [L1] yield $|((c+h)^n-c^n)/h|\le nR^{n-1}$. Thus the tail of the difference-quotient series beyond degree $N$ is at most $\sum_{n>N}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$, uniformly for these $h$. The tail of the proposed derivative series at $c$ has the same bound. [given, L1, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: Fix $c$ with $|c|<R_0$ and choose $R$ with $|c|<R<R_0$. For $0<|h|<R-|c|$, the identity $$ (c+h)^n-c^n=h\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(c+h)^{n-1-j}c^j $$ for $n\ge1$ and [L1] yield $|((c+h)^n-c^n)/h|\le nR^{n-1}$. Thus the tail of the difference-quotient series beyond degree $N$ is at most $\sum_{n>N}n|a_n|R^{n-1}$, uniformly for these $h$. The tail of the proposed derivative series at $c$ has the same bound.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For fixed $N$, the difference quotient of the polynomial $\sum_{n=0}^N a_nx^n$ tends to $\sum_{n=1}^Nna_nc^{n-1}$ as $h\to0$ by the binomial identity. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so both tails bounded above are below $\varepsilon/3$, then choose $h$ small enough that the finite polynomial quotient differs from its derivative by less than $\varepsilon/3$. The full difference quotient therefore differs from $\sum_{n\ge1}na_nc^{n-1}$ by less than $\varepsilon$, proving the derivative formula. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For fixed $N$, the difference quotient of the polynomial $\sum_{n=0}^N a_nx^n$ tends to $\sum_{n=1}^Nna_nc^{n-1}$ as $h\to0$ by the binomial identity. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so both tails bounded above are below $\varepsilon/3$, then choose $h$ small enough that the finite polynomial quotient differs from its derivative by less than $\varepsilon/3$. The full difference quotient therefore differs from $\sum_{n\ge1}na_nc^{n-1}$ by less than $\varepsilon$, proving the derivative formula.

items.assessment: For the main a<b case the partition family contains the two-endpoint partition and every partition has at least one subinterval. The proof uses actual attained extrema and common refinements; the Statement separately defines coincident-endpoint integral zero and reversed orientation. Thus an empty partition is unnecessary, and the degenerate integral extension is explicit.

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right| \le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For a partition $P$, the maxima and minima in its sums exist by [L2]. If $Q$ refines $P$, each old subinterval is divided into finitely many pieces; the minimum on each piece is at least the old minimum and the maximum is at most the old maximum. Since the piece lengths sum to the old length, $L(g,P)\le L(g,Q)\le U(g,Q)\le U(g,P)$. [given, L2, algebra]
complete_current_proof_blocks.claim: For a partition $P$, the maxima and minima in its sums exist by [L2]. If $Q$ refines $P$, each old subinterval is divided into finitely many pieces; the minimum on each piece is at least the old minimum and the maximum is at most the old maximum. Since the piece lengths sum to the old length, $L(g,P)\le L(g,Q)\le U(g,Q)\le U(g,P)$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $x\in[a,b]$, continuity [F2] gives $\delta_x>0$ such that $|g(t)-g(x)|<\varepsilon/2$ when $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta_x$. The relative neighborhoods $(x-\delta_x/2,x+\delta_x/2)\cap[a,b]$ cover $[a,b]$. Choose a finite subcover with centers $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ by [L1], and put $\delta=\min_i\delta_{x_i}/2>0$. If $u,v\in[a,b]$, $|u-v|<\delta$, and $u$ belongs to the neighborhood centered at $x_i$, then both $u$ and $v$ are within $\delta_{x_i}$ of $x_i$. By [L4], $|g(u)-g(v)|\le|g(u)-g(x_i)|+|g(v)-g(x_i)|<\varepsilon$. Thus $g$ is uniformly continuous. [given, F2, L1, L4, choose]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The range of $g$ has a minimum $m$ and maximum $M$ by [L2]. Thus all lower and upper sums lie between $m(b-a)$ and $M(b-a)$, and the partition set is nonempty. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apply step 1.2 with tolerance $\varepsilon/(2(b-a))$ and choose an equal partition with mesh smaller than its uniform-continuity radius, using [L3]. On each piece the oscillation $\max g-\min g$ is less than that tolerance, because both extrema are attained by [L2]. Hence $U(g,P)-L(g,P)<\varepsilon/2$. Since $I_-\ge L(g,P)$ and $I_+\le U(g,P)$, we have $0\le I_+-I_-<\varepsilon$. This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $I_-=I_+$. Their common value defines the integral in the statement. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $c$ with $a<c<b$. Refining any partition by inserting $c$ cannot increase its upper sum by step 1.1, so the infimum of upper sums over all partitions equals the infimum over partitions containing $c$. Each such upper sum is the sum of an upper sum on $[a,c]$ and one on $[c,b]$. Every pair of partitions of these two intervals combines to a partition containing $c$; therefore the infimum of the combined sums is the sum of the two separate infima (choose each sum within $\varepsilon/2$ of its infimum for the reverse inequality). The common upper/lower values from step 2.2 give $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. Endpoint cases follow from $\int_a^a g=0$. Reversal is the definition, so the integral is oriented and additive. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The constant function with value $d$ has every upper and lower sum equal to $d(b-a)$, so its integral is $d(b-a)$. More generally, if constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, every lower sum is at least $m(b-a)$ and every upper sum is at most $M(b-a)$; hence $m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$. If $m_0$ and $M_0$ are the attained minimum and maximum of $g$, then $C:=\max(|m_0|,|M_0|)=\max_{t\in[a,b]}|g(t)|$, since every value lies between $m_0$ and $M_0$. Applying the comparison with $m=-C,M=C$ gives $|\int_a^b g|\le C(b-a)$; reversal gives the bound with $|b-a|$ for either orientation. [given, L2, step 2.2, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $g$ be continuous on an open interval $J$, fix $x_0\in J$, and put $G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$. The compact-segment results above define each integral. By additivity from step 3.1 and the constant-integral calculation in step 3.2, for $h\ne0$ sufficiently small, $$\frac{G(x+h)-G(x)}h =\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}g(t)\,dt.$$ For any $\eta>0$, continuity at $x$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $g(x)-\eta<g(t)<g(x)+\eta$ whenever $|t-x|<\delta$. If $-\delta<h<0$, reverse the integral by step 3.1, apply the same comparison on $[x+h,x]$, and divide by the negative $h$; the inequalities again place the quotient between those same constants. The extrema of $g$ on each such segment exist by [L2], and the largest deviation from $g(x)$ is attained at one of them. Hence its limit is $g(x)$, so $G'(x)=g(x)$. items.assessment: The Definition uses fixed natural-indexed power series and continuous integrals on the segment between specified endpoints. Coincident integral endpoints give zero by the oriented integral supplier, but no empty coefficient index set is an input. Logarithm/reciprocal/tangent/principal-argument domains and excluded branch cases are explicit, not arbitrary point-function choices.

claim_sections.Definition:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\ \pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

items.assessment: The Statement fixes N>=1, so each truncated series has at least two terms, while its infinite tails start at the next actual index. The proof handles transformed zero arguments and logarithm at one separately and keeps every geometric denominator positive on the stated reduced domains. No empty-series truncation is claimed.

claim_sections.Statement:
For $|u|\le1/2$ and integer $N\ge1$, set
$E_N(u)=\sum_{k=0}^N u^k/k!$ and
$R_E=|u|^{N+1}/((N+1)!(1-|u|/(N+2)))$. Then
$\exp(u)\in[E_N(u)-R_E,E_N(u)+R_E]$, and the lower endpoint is positive.
For $y\in[1,2]$, put $v=(y-1)/(y+1)$ and
$L_N(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^N v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$\left|\ln y-L_N(v)\right|\le \frac{2|v|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-v^2)}.$$
For every integer $j$ and $y>0$, the natural logarithm also satisfies
$\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$.
For $|t|\le1/2$, set $A_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^kt^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Then
$$\left|\arctan t-A_N(t)\right|\le \frac{|t|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)(1-t^2)}.$$

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $k\ge N+1$, consecutive absolute exponential terms have ratio $|u|/(k+1)\le q:=|u|/(N+2)<1$. Their tail is bounded by the first omitted term times $1+q+q^2+\cdots=1/(1-q)$, giving $R_E$. The defining power series lies between its partial sum plus or minus this absolute tail. For $N\ge1$, the partial sum is at least $1-|u|\ge1/2$ by alternating-series grouping when $u<0$ and by positivity when $u\ge0$; also $R_E\le(1/2)^2/(2(1-1/6))=3/20<1/2$. Thus the lower bound is positive. [given, L1, L5, L6, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For $y\in[1,2]$, $v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. Set $G(v)=2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$. Its derivative series is absolutely convergent for $|v|<1$ by [L6], so [L4] gives $G'(v)=2/(1-v^2)$. By [L3], $H(y)=G(v(y))$ has derivative $4/((y+1)^2(1-v^2))=1/y$. The integral definition [L1] has derivative $1/y$, since its difference quotient is the average of the continuous integrand $1/t$ near $y$; also $H(1)=\ln1=0$. For $y>1$, apply [L2] to $H-\ln$ on $[1,y]$; its derivative is zero, so $H(y)-\ln y=H(1)-\ln1=0$. Equality at $y=1$ holds by the integral definition. Hence $H(y)=\ln y$ on $[1,2]$. complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $y>0$ and let $h(x)=\ln(xy)-\ln x$ for $x>0$. From [L1], the integral difference quotient gives $(\ln x)'=1/x$. The chain rule [L3] therefore gives $h'(x)=y/(xy)-1/x=0$. Applying [L2] on the positive segment between $1$ and any $x>0$ shows $h(x)=h(1)=\ln y$, so $\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y$. Repeated use gives the identity for positive integer powers of $2$; applying it to $2\cdot(1/2)=1$ gives $\ln(1/2)=-\ln2$, hence the same identity for negative integer powers and $j=0$. Thus $\ln(2^j y)=j\ln2+\ln y$ for every integer $j$. [given, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Fix $x\ne c$ and set $A=(f(x)-P_n(x))/(x-c)^{n+1}$ and $g(t)=f(t)-P_n(t)-A(t-c)^{n+1}$ on the interval between $c$ and $x$. Then $g(c)=g(x)=0$ and $g^{(j)}(c)=0$ for each $1\le j\le n$, because the Taylor polynomial matches those derivatives at $c$ by [L2] and the last term has a zero of order $n+1$. [given, L2, construct, algebra]

claim_sections.Statement:
Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For fixed $f,c,x$, define $I_m=\frac1{m!}\int_c^x f^{(m+1)}(t)(x-t)^m\,dt$ for $0\le m\le n$. For $m=0$, [L1] gives $I_0=f(x)-f(c)$. For $m\ge1$, apply integration by parts [L1] to $u(t)=f^{(m)}(t)$ and $v(t)=(x-t)^m/m!$. Since $v(x)=0$, $v(c)=(x-c)^m/m!$, and $v'(t)=-(x-t)^{m-1}/(m-1)!$, it gives $$ I_m=I_{m-1}-\frac{f^{(m)}(c)(x-c)^m}{m!}. $$ Induction from $I_0$ yields $I_n=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(x-c)^j/j!=f(x)-P_n(x)$. The oriented integration-by-parts identity makes the same recurrence valid when $x<c$; if $x=c$, both sides are zero. [given, F1, L1, algebra, induction]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Let $d=|x-c|$ and $\psi(t)=f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n/n!$. This is continuous. The triangle inequality in [L3], applied in both directions, gives $\bigl||\psi(s)|-|\psi(t)|\bigr|\le|\psi(s)-\psi(t)|$, so $|\psi|$ is continuous too and both functions are integrable. By [L2] and [L4], the integral is monotone in the integrand, so $$\left|\int_c^x\psi(t)\,dt\right| \le\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|\psi(t)|\,dt \le\frac{M}{n!}\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|x-t|^n\,dt.$$ The first inequality follows by integrating $-|\psi|\le\psi\le|\psi|$ on the forward interval and using $\int(-|\psi|)=-\int|\psi|$; orientation does not change the absolute value. The last power integral is $d^{n+1}/(n+1)$ by [L1], using its polynomial antiderivative on the segment to either side of $x$. Thus the bound is $Md^{n+1}/(n+1)!$. Combining this with step 1.1 proves the result. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.assessment: The proof uses finite fixed-term series with nonzero integer factorial denominators and sound rational tail formulas on their reduced domains. It separately returns split/nonfinite status when tangent's cosine may vanish. Zero inputs and constant/zero-width enclosures are admitted through the primitive range rules, while uncertified domains carry no finite success claim.

claim_sections.Statement:
Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For an exponential input interval, the fixed scale puts every scaled point in $[-1/2,1/2]$. The point bound [L3] with $|u|$ replaced by the interval's largest absolute endpoint gives a uniform tail enclosure. The truncated polynomial interval-evaluates every point by [L2]. The tail radius increases with the largest absolute input, and each repeated interval square preserves inclusion by [L2]. To justify the scaling identity, put $d=2^s$. Repeated applications of [L6] to the absolutely convergent series for $\exp u$ show that the coefficient of $u^k$ in $(\exp u)^d$ is $$\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_d=k}\frac1{n_1!\cdots n_d!} =\frac{d^k}{k!},$$ where the equality is the multinomial theorem. Thus $(\exp u)^d=\exp(du)$; set $u=x/d$. Each interval squaring preserves the resulting enclosure by [L2]. [given, L1, L2, L3, L6, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: The outward cell interval built from $P_N$ contains each exact canonical cell, since $\pi\in P_N$; thus its intersection hull $X_k$ contains every input point assigned to that cell, and $X_k-kP_N/2$ contains the exact residual $r=x-k\pi/2$. The algorithm certifies this residual inside the Taylor range. By [L4], exact sine and cosine values are the stated signed swaps of $\sin r$ and $\cos r$. The polynomial interval evaluation contains each truncated value by [L2], and adding the symmetric tail interval from [L4] contains the omitted remainder. Taking the hull over all intersected cells therefore contains the full range. If the interval width is at least $2\pi$, [L4] gives the safe range $[-1,1]$. For nested inputs, each fixed canonical cell intersection enlarges and its fixed-term interval evaluation is isotone by [L2]; the hull is therefore nested on the reduced branch. Exact rational interval polynomial and tail operations are inclusion-isotone, and the final directed endpoint conversions are nondecreasing. Intersecting with $[-1,1]$ preserves containment and nesting, and ensures that the wide-input $[-1,1]$ return contains every narrower finite result. [given, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: On each positive logarithm bin, every $y$ maps to $v=(y-1)/(y+1)\in[0,1/3]$. The interval series and uniform tail from [L3] contain $\ln y$; [L3] also proves the exact logarithm scaling identity used by the algorithm. Each interval transform and sum preserves inclusion by [L2]. The fixed bin partition ensures that enlarging the input only enlarges the intersection with each bin, so its interval-series enclosure and the final hull also enlarge. The arctangent transformations follow from [L5]; on each fixed branch the rational interval maps and fixed series are isotone, and the tail radius is nondecreasing in the largest absolute transformed endpoint. items.assessment: The Statement and imported algorithm use a nonempty categorical list. Its proof treats clipped cumulative thresholds including zero/one and separately proves zero search updates at r=1 and immediate return for input zero. All count and search operations are finite and specified; the bound does not claim a biconditional.

claim_sections.Statement: For the finite categorical procedure of [[alg-finite-categorical-inverse-cdf]], ideal uniform input gives exact probability $p_i$ to outcome $i$. For $b$-bit midpoint input, each cumulative threshold frequency differs from its target $C_i$ by at most $2^{-b-1}$, and each individual outcome frequency differs from $p_i$ by at most $2^{-b}$. The ordered binary search terminates at the stated least index, using at most $\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$ cumulative-array comparisons on a positive input; its explicit zero-input branch returns outcome $1$.

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Apart from the null event $U=0$, outcome $i$ is returned exactly when $C_{i-1}<U\le C_i$, an interval of length $C_i-C_{i-1}=p_i$. Its uniform probability is the interval length $C_i-C_{i-1}=p_i$, so the ideal law is exactly the specified categorical law. [given, F2, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: Put $N=2^b$. For any threshold $C\in[0,1]$, the number of midpoints $(k+1/2)/N\le C$ is $\min(N,\max(0,\lfloor NC+1/2\rfloor))$. Thus its normalized count differs from $C$ by at most $1/(2N)$. Applying this to $C_i$ and $C_{i-1}$, the frequency of outcome $i$ is the difference of their cumulative frequencies, so its error from $p_i$ is at most $1/N=2^{-b}$. [F1, F2, A1, algebra]

complete_current_proof_blocks.text: For positive $v\le1=C_r$, the least admissible index exists. Initially it lies in $[L,H]=[1,r]$. If $v\le C_j$, monotonicity of the cumulative sums puts that index in $[L,j]$; otherwise it lies in $[j+1,H]$. Thus both updates preserve the invariant, and at $L=H$ the returned index is the least admissible one. When the interval contains $n>1$ indices, $j=\lfloor(L+H)/2\rfloor$ leaves at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ indices and uses one cumulative-array comparison. After $k$ updates at most $\lceil r/2^k\rceil$ remain, by induction; at $k=\lceil\log_2r\rceil$ this is one. When $r=1$ the loop has zero updates. The zero-input branch returns immediately as specified. [given, F2, algebra, induction] ∎
